 The northern snow fell like Death's scythe;
 
 Could it ever suffer two peoples in peace?
 
 Golden hair dishevelled, silver goblets overturned, iron armour rent.
 
 Swords clamoured loud, driving ever closer upon the Solarian guests.
 
 Arrows sped in volleys, hounding the Solarian like a hunted pack of wolves.

res.name: Silvercandle Hymn (Ⅵ)
res.text:
Ⅵ. The Snow-Owl's Ballad, Canto Ⅲ
 
 The snow-owl wept, the snow-owl cried,
 
 Nine times it wheeled through the nighted sky.
 
 It longed to flee the tumult —
 
 Yet cunning are the demons,
 
 Who beguile not only the bewildered bird.
 
 Even Dis Galea, who once struck down a false god,
 
 Deemed himself scorned by Fate,
 
 Doomed to an end unimagined.
 
 Only one carved a path through the tightening snare of the Charon:
 
 Soranus Galea, blazing with wrath at deceit.
 
 In fury he cast a burning candelabrum as a spear, piercing the armour of his foes.
 
 In defiance he swung a brimming silver goblet as a hammer, shattering the helms of the wicked.
 
 Before him, the Charon fell in heaps;
 
 Behind him, stretched a road of blood and flesh.
 
 It was he who had once knocked upon that door,
 
 And so he swore he would depart in whole.
 
 Dis Galea followed close behind,
 
 As though clawing free from a demon's ravenous maw.
 
 He rejoiced that his banner yet stood, unswallowed by the snow.
 
 But Soranus had spent his final strength.
 
 The demons overtook him, their blades came down,
 
 And from that noble brow there burst a white flame.
 
 The glacier crumbled, blood welled forth, hardening into stones of crimson agate.
 
 So fell Soranus Galea, sole brother of Dis Ⅰ.
 
 On the day the Great Migration began, he had sworn to march hand in hand with Death.
 
 Yet none foresaw that Fate would on this day bare its fangs in laughter.
 
 And the snow-owl, too, seeking its feast,
 
 Was struck by an accursed arrow,
 
 Its breath lost amid the bloodied waters.
 
 Alas! Soranus — hero who called for peace...
 
 He never lived to behold the birth of the Hyperborean Empire,
 
 Yet he became its first and truest hero.

res.name: Silvercandle Hymn (Ⅶ)
res.text:
Ⅶ. The Proclamation of Vengeance
 
 Dis Galea returned into the snowbound wilderness.
 
 Words forsook him; darkness veiled his sight without end.
 
 In silence he recalled his brother's face.
 
 Had he yet trod the sacred halls of Elysium,
 
 He would have cried aloud the names of the Great Nine,
 
 Entreating the power that guides the fallen home.
 
 But blind faith was long renounced, the idols cast down,
 
 And death itself bore witness: the gods were gone.
 
 So the host kept silence, and with Dis Galea they mourned wordlessly.
 
 The soldiers, wrath bound in silence, awaited his command.
 
 The frozen earth trembled beneath his wrath.
 
 Three days and three nights his silence endured.
 
 The host waited, and waited still — for their lord to call forth vengeance, to cast the demons into dust.
 
 At last he spoke, slow and measured: "Leave these snows. Let us bide our time.
 
 The Charon are indeed our foes; yet more loathsome still is our own frailty.
 
 The demons bear no Solarian virtue. They wield their strength in wanton excess.
 
 Then must we forge a strength redoubled, to cast them down and bind them fast in chains.
 
 Better to gather strength, to lie low in wait for a just vengeance,
 
 Than to squander rage to our common ruin."

res.name: Silvercandle Hymn (Ⅷ)
res.text:
Ⅷ. The Iron Hooves in Their Charge
 
 The host stirred and swelled like waters brought to the boil.
 
 Far-sighted was Dis Galea,
 
 Prudent was Dis Galea!
 
 And so they mourned with Dis Galea for Solanus,
 
 For Solanus, revered and feared, had fallen.
 
 Dirges rose and tears fell,
 
 As though a thousand stars descended all at once.
 
 The night lay veiled in mist; no guiding star remained.
 
 This day we endure the bitterness of deceit;
 
 Yet when the tide of the Great Migration next sweeps the snowbound plain:
 
 Though death descends as equal fate on every soul, Sola and Charon alike,
 
 The demons' blood shall drench the earth.
 
 Their bones shall be wrought into goblets;
 
 Their houses shall become graveyards;
 
 Their horns shall be broken and cast into Lamenting Lake, until its waters brim with ruin.
 
 And this land, bright with Phoxene, shall rise as offering unto Soranus.
 
 Thus, feeding on hatred,
 
 Dis Galea and his host endured the winter.
 
 They unsheathed their swords and seized the hamlets;
 
 They tightened their reins and trampled the houses.
 
 Yet endless massacre slowly dulled their wrath,
 
 And the Solarian, guided by reason, turned from the path of carnage and blood, 
 
 And sought instead a road of concord.

res.name: Silvercandle Hymn (Ⅸ)
res.text:
Ⅸ. The Dissolving of Hatred
 
 Ten times did the ice of Lamenting Lake melt, and ten times it froze anew.
 
 And in the villages the Charon's dread deepened day by day —
 
 For ten years past it was they who had plotted a massacre that failed,
 
 And it was they who must now taste its bitter fruit.
 
 Dis Galea, clinging to life by Fate's frail thread,
 
 Endured the harsh winters of the North by means unknown,
 
 And with the silver tide of his host he laid waste to every land round about.
 
 At last he came,
 
 And with his coming an ending surely fell.
 
 With his host he cast down in swift might the fortress reared upon Soranus's grave.
 
 The Charon, in despair, murmured prayers to Mother Embla,
 
 Believing that this day would see them sink into the Misty Sea's embrace.
 
 Yet what came was neither slaughter nor conquest,
 
 But leniency beyond all measure.
 
 Dis Galea cursed Fate,
 
 Yet ten years of war had bent his heart toward peace.
 
 In his letters he wrote thus, grave and rational:
 
 "Vengeance is scarlet, fair to behold — yet it only ends in withering.
 
 Peace is silver, grievous to bear — yet it composes the song of prosperity.
 
 Even if we let the Charon's blood sink into the stone, yet the stone shall one day crumble to desert.
 
 But once the seeds of peace are sown, for centuries, for millennia, flowers shall bloom."
 
 "My Solarian brothers, burdened with hatred — let us together cast scorn upon Fate.
 
 To deny anger its dominion over the mind — that is the very proof of our humanity.
 
 These Charon, once branded Children of the Demon, 
 
 Are righteous folk who rose against the Church.
 
 Rather than cross swords and raise the dirge,
 
 Let Soranus be the first and last sacrifice.
 
 And the Charon shall mourn him with us as sisters and brothers.
 
 So long as Lamenting Lake endures,
 
 So long as the mountains stand,
 
 The name of Soranus shall be sung without end, echoing between mountain and lake.

res.name: Silvercandle Hymn (Ⅹ)
res.text:
Ⅹ. Silver Candles Aflame, the Carnival Begins
 
 Thus did Galea's soldiers, the Solarian host who had reached the uttermost North,
 
 Lay down their swords, set aside their hatred,
 
 And lifted silver candles on high with hearts of mercy.
 
 Following close upon Galea, they came unto the dwellings of the Charon.
 
 White mountains stretched, the keen winds howled,
 
 And the Charon, who thought the flame of war was at hand, beheld instead from afar the silver candlelight.
 
 They marvelled: the Solarian host comes not for vengeance, but for peace!
 
 Dis I had lost a brother;
 
 Yet were not the Charon themselves a vaster host of brethren?
 
 Then the Charon brought forth their finest wine,
 
 With meats newly cured and berries preserved.
 
 They pledged kinship with Dis I,
 
 And hailed the gracious, gentle Galea as their lord.
 
 They raised a city meant to endure — 
 
 Walls, a great plaza, lofty halls, and a theatre of song.
 
 There, Solarian and Charon alike
 
 Would share their finest days without divide.
 
 All who heard Dis I proclaim that vision were enthralled;
 
 And each vowed to be the cornerstone of the Empire's enduring dream.
 
 From that day, with each returning year, 
 
 In Icelake — where Soranus fell and the tragedy found its end — 
 
 The people gather.
 
 They kindle candles in silver candlesticks,
 
 And strike the festival's first note in the Far North.
 
 The flames soar, recalling ages past;
 
 The bells resound long, and grief is cast away.
 
 So hear — hear the songs that shall never fade;
 
 Sing — sing the hymn to the everlasting Empire.

name: Boycott the Silvercandle Carnival!
desc: A hand-scrawled flyer, its jagged script so fierce you can almost hear it shouting. Line by line it denounces the Silvercandle Hymn, proclaiming the truth turned on its head.

res.text:
Charon brothers, Charon sisters — remember that verse they drilled into us when we were kids?
"Have you heard of such a carnival, where blasphemers clasp the hands of Demon's Children?"
Yeah, that one. The Silvercandle Hymn. We've heard it so many times our ears grew numb.
Every year, when that day comes, we Charon — scraping through bitter lives — stitch together masks and costumes. Because only then do the Solarian pretend to treat us as human. Only then do they hold back their scorn. They dance, they laugh — and they blast that cursed Hymn at us a hundred times over.
And I know many of you can recite its lines, maybe even feel sorry for the "kind-hearted" Dis I and his brother Soranus. Some even believe — because our ancestors supposedly killed Soranus — that we're bound to serve the Solarian forever. They say it's our destiny. To repay a blood debt. I say that's all lies.
Don't buy it.
Don't buy it!
Don't buy it!!!
The Silvercandle Carnival is a lie from start to finish. There never was a carnival. Only a massacre. And Soranus? He wasn't some poor victim. He was the butcher — the worst of them all!
 
Listen, I'll tell you another story. The truth.
 
Our ancestors, the Charon, lived in the North. Because of Deterioration, they didn't build great cities — just small scattered villages. One clan lived by Lamenting Lake, warming themselves with Phoxene from the Heaventree nearby, living on what little they had.
Then came rumours from the South — trouble in the Elysian Church, rebels driven out, exiles wandering north. At first it was just gossip. Elysium was too far to matter. Until Solarian soldiers showed up, armed, on our lake shore.
Our ancestors pitied them. Thought they'd never survive the northern winter. So they took them in, gave them food.
That winter was cruel, as if Father Ask and Mother Embla cursed us with the storm. But the cold didn't kill them — it only fed their greed. Galea, their leader, seemed harmless enough. But his brother? A greedy wolf. The first time he stepped into the village, his eyes went straight to our granaries. Already he was thinking of plunder.
And on the night meant for peace, that brute Soranus had his blades and shields ready. At the feast our ancestors prepared, he struck.
By dawn, except for a handful of hunters out in the wilds, none were left alive... Galea built Icelake on our ancestors' graves, and from it rose his Empire. His men enslaved us, lied to us, branded us sinners.
 
Think about it! Really think about it! The Hymn — every line is about the Solarian. Not once does it name a single Charon. Why? Because they didn't know? Or because they never cared?
The Silvercandle Carnival? A sham. The Hymn? Lies. They boast, "On this day we're equal; on this day we dance together." Liars! That wall between Solarian and Charon? They built it! And Soranus? He wasn't a hero or martyr. He was a filthy butcher!
Don't be fooled. Boycott the Silvercandle Carnival!

name: What'll It Be? Just Say the Word!
desc: The Asphodel's drinks menu — every glass, full-bodied and fragrant. One sip, and you'll be back for more.

res.text:
Welcome to The Asphodel. Our tavern serves drinks from every corner of the continent. And don't worry — we always collect the coin before you pass out.
 
 The Hyperborean Empire:
 Most of our Empire's brews find their way into the bellies of alchemists and soldiers, so the names may not sound drinkable... yet the taste is finer than you'd think. Craving something strong? Just say the word!
 Legion Wolfblood
 Standard issue across the Legions — a spirit strong enough to burn off fear on the battlefield and double as a battlefield disinfectant. The taste is strong — deliberately so, they say, to stop soldiers from overindulging.
 
 Phoxichor Engine Lubricant
 A favourite among Imperial alchemists. Named for its uncanny resemblance — in both colour and texture — to the actual lubricant used in Phoxichor engines. Rumour has it one absent-minded alchemist once took a swig of the real thing by mistake.
 
 Fortress Barrage
 A fiery spirit from the Empire's southern reaches. Best downed in one go to savour the full effect — like a fortress cannon blasting through your body, leaving your limbs no longer your own. Intense. Devastating. Glorious.
 
 Laurelled Delight
 The go-to toast when a Charon earns their Laurel. Often shaken into a froth for the ceremony — but beneath the bubbles lies a crisp, refreshing flavour, delightful on the tongue.
 
 Huaxu:
 If spirits are too strong for your taste, why not try something from the Eastern realm? Unlike the grape wines we know, theirs are brewed from rice — smooth, mellow, and golden as amber. And with Huaxu's travelling merchants scattered far and wide, these delicacies are never far from hand. In the mood for something different? Just say the word!
 Tiger's Soul
 An amber-hued rice wine with a rich, mellow depth — said to carry the essence of a tiger's spirit. In Huaxu, it is a common daily draught, a medicinal tonic, and a warming comfort all in one.
 
 Peach Blush
 A light, sweet wine with the fragrance of fresh fruit. Blended with peach gum, its texture is as soft to chew as it is to sip. Its delicate blush has long made it a favourite among ladies.
 
 A Goblet Above
 A Huaxu proverb says: "One day above is a year below." True to its name, a single goblet of this potent brew sends you into a deep slumber — and when you wake, much time will have fled. Best not overindulge — lest you find yourself in Heaven sooner than you wished.
 
 Azure Dragon's Draught
 In Huaxu, the Charon are honoured as Loongscions — descendants of the Eastern dragon. This is their drink of choice: crisp as a mountain spring, with a finish that lingers like the breath of a Loong.
 
 Republic of Luca:
 You may know Luca for its artists, sailors, dreamers and madcaps... but did you know it also gave birth to a world of cocktails? Try them, and you'll be won over by their rich layers and flights of fancy. They rarely leave one truly drunk... but they do have a way of stirring inspiration. So, what shall it be? Just say the word!
 Palette
 A cascade of spirits, layered in dazzling colours — a painting in a glass. Stir it, and all brilliance collapses into black.
 
 Masquerade Rhapsody
 Not one drink, but ten — each wearing the same disguise. You won't know what lies within until you taste it... just as you never truly know the face behind a mask at the ball.
 
 Poet's Rhyme
 Soft upon the tongue, yet echoing long after — like the rhyme that closes a verse. Poets and playwrights drink deep in pursuit of inspiration... sometimes yielding a masterpiece, and sometimes, a grand puddle of vomit.
 
 Chisel
 A rare Luca spirit, named by sailors who once gazed upon statues crated in their holds and thought of the tool that shaped them. True to its name, it etches fire through the body with each swallow.
 
 Aethyrie:
 Do scholars drink? Indeed they do. They drink to dull the sting of failure... and to raise a jubilant toast with a ringing "Eureka!" when discovery strikes. Like knowledge, wine intoxicates all the same. The only pity is that even in naming it, they cannot resist teaching a lesson. If such hidden meanings amuse you — just say the word.
 Truth in the Cup
 Aethyrie's scholars once argued fiercely over the world's first principle — some claimed it was air, others fire, others still countless tiny particles. At last, they agreed on one thing: whatever its origin, it must be plentiful in wine, for nothing else so swiftly brings joy, and peace among rivals.
 
 Philosopher's Tears
 One tale tells of a philosopher who, upon realising that the diagonal of a square vessel could not be expressed by rational number, wept until his tears ran dry, and bled instead. Thus, the crimson hue of this wine. Aethyrie's scholars adore the tale. Of course, the truth is simpler and far less poignant: it's just the colour of grapes.
 
 O, Bounty!
 Brewed only in years of true abundance, this wine heralds the coming of plenty. Once the vats are filled, the people of Aethyrie gather in celebration — drinking deep, lifting their voices in song or spirited debate, rejoicing in the bounty of the year.
 
 The Syllogism
 Major premise: wine brings inspiration.
 Minor premise: inspiration is the wellspring of creation.
 Conclusion: wine is the wellspring of creation.
 In Aethyrie, only students sharp enough to name the fallacy earn the right to drink it. Luckily for you, here in Hyperborea, no riddle need be solved before your glass is filled.
 
 Khemet:
 Life in the desert is harsh, its people rugged — yet their welcome is as warm as the sands are fierce. When Starweavers or Phoxhunters pass through their villages, the locals pour out drinks as bold and mysterious as the desert itself. This tavern may not lie among the dunes, but our welcome is no less hearty. Care to taste the desert wind? Just say the word!
 Black Honey
 Dark as pitch, yet heavy with sweetness. Its deep shade comes from carbon — said to draw out every impurity.
 
 Serpent's Kiss
 Rumoured to be laced with snake venom, it numbs the tongue with a venomous tingle and chills the body with a creeping cool. In truth, it's nothing but fizzing gases.
 
 Experimental Dregs
 A dangerous concoction brewed from industrial alcohol and leftover dregs of countless alchemical experiments. They say you might find a lizard's claw or rat's tail adrift within. Only the daring drink it — more a test of courage than a toast.
 
 The Burning Wind
 Steeped with spice and peppers, this fiery brew scours the throat like the desert wind itself. One mouthful, and you're carried to Khemet's sands in all their scorching glory.
 
 The Elysian Church:
 To the south lies the Elysian Church — the Empire's sworn foe. Its folk drown in scripture, bowing to false gods in blind faith... hopeless, if you ask me. But their wines — now those are worth a taste. Rare, costly, and hard to come by. If your purse is heavy enough, just say the word!
 The Tenth God
 The war with Elysium grinds on, and so their wares are forbidden in the Empire. Even so, one brew still finds its way to our shelves: The Tenth God. It's named in jest — as if one drink could rival the blessings of all nine gods. Perhaps that sly irreverence is why the officials turned a blind eye — a blasphemous name, for a drink too fine to ban.
 
 Traditional Charon Brews:
 The mountains beyond the Empire's northern edge are not empty. There, the Charon who still defy its yoke dwell — honouring their Father Ask and Mother Embla. They brew their own drinks for rites that preserve their faith and legend. Sometimes, these brews are traded for a handful of coins. They're not strong, but in Icelake's biting cold, nothing warms you better. If you'd warm your bones — and hear a tale of the Charon — just say the word!
 Heaventree Sap
 A light, clear blue liquor that recalls the gleam of Phoxene. Unlike Phoxichor Engine Lubricant, it runs bright and fluid. Its name honours the Heaventrees — sacred to Charon tradition.
 
 Borealberry Brew
 Brewed from Borealberries — a prized fruit of Icelake and the far north — this wine is fragrant and best enjoyed steaming hot. The Charon may not fear the cold, but none would turn down a sweet, steaming glass of fruit-rich delight in the heart of winter.
 
 
 We don't serve minors. And don't bother with "it's for my parents" — that tale's worn thin.
 Also, no vomiting in the tavern. You'll pay for the cleaning... and we'll throw in a good thrashing, free of charge.

name: Secret Histories of the Forsakens
desc: Rumours of the Forsakens' upper echelons — their credibility uncertain, but entertaining enough for a light read.

res.name: Secret Histories of the Forsakens (Ⅰ)
res.text:
The "Benefactor" — so named for their role as giver — is one of the few Forsaken leaders whose existence can be confirmed. True to their name, they are famed for immense wealth. Before we go further, two points must be made clear: first, the Forsakens are not a profit-driven organisation; second, most of their members possess no honest livelihood.
 
Indeed, the Forsakens care little for profit — their focus lies squarely in undermining the order of the Hyperborean Empire. Other resistance groups may raid treasuries or stage kidnappings for ransom, but the Forsakens have never stooped to such schemes. This makes them easy to distinguish: if a crime was committed for money, it likely wasn't their doing. The Forsakens care only for destruction. Alchemy factories, interregional roads, and the manors of prominent officials are among their favourite targets. Some claim this pattern reflects a kind of moral fastidiousness in their founders. I cannot agree. Morality restrains those who revere rules — but given the Forsakens' origins and conduct, one can hardly argue that morality plays any meaningful part in shaping them.
 
According to statistics gathered by Warden Hellfire, at least half the Forsaken members now imprisoned had already been convicted of other crimes before joining the organisation. Thugs, petty thieves, armed robbers — criminals unmoved by the law, let alone by morality. Yet once inside the Forsakens, none of them committed crimes for money alone. This can only mean the organisation upholds a code more binding than law — and possesses financial resources sufficient to sustain its members' lives, even to fuel their crimes. From this, Warden Hellfire drew a prediction: among the Forsakens' leaders, there must be one who bears the cost of the organisation's daily needs. As the Forsakens grew active again and more members were thrown behind bars, a certain codename began surfacing in warden reports — "Benefactor."
 
The "Benefactor" is said to reach out in one's hour of deepest desperation, sending a letter with whatever the recipient most craves. Most often it is money; at times, something bloodier — a grisly token of vengeance, such as the severed limb of a sworn enemy. Though recipients may technically refuse these sudden acts of generosity, the timing is so uncannily precise that in practice, no one ever does. And so, wastrels and dangerous marauders alike find themselves drawn into the Forsakens. When their old vices drag them back into hardship, another letter arrives. After several such cycles, they become puppets — marionettes strung with coin, dancing at the Benefactor's whim. The tasks assigned differ little from their former crimes. A thief is told to break the chains on an alchemy factory gate. A bomber, to plant charges beside its Phoxichor engine. A repeat escapee, to present himself before the constables — drawing their attention elsewhere. Thus, strangers who've never met, acting solely on the direction of letters from a single hand, carry out crimes near impossible to unravel. None of them knows whether they have accomplices, whether they're the bait in someone else's scheme, or what the mission's true purpose might be. Such is the Benefactor's method. Though their schemes leave ample traces, the Benefactor makes no real effort to conceal their presence. To the wardens, each letter sent to an underling reads like an open declaration of war. And so, in the years when the Benefactor was most active, wardens across the Hyperborean Empire poured untold hours into unmasking them.
 
In theory, it should have been simple. The Benefactor's letters came with great sums of money — and wealth, after all, leaves a trail. Soon enough, the wardens caught a supposed Benefactor: a cloth merchant in Scarletriver who had recently struck it rich. He claimed he had taken up the name out of outrage at the Empire's oppression of the Charon, and that his crimes were acts of rebellion. To any clear-eyed observer, it was a flimsy excuse. No ordinary merchant could bankroll a resistance force spanning the continent. This "Benefactor" was nothing but a decoy — a scapegoat. So the wardens pressed on. One captured, then another... more than ten in all, over the span of two years. Yet the Forsakens' resistance showed no sign of waning. There could be no doubt: above these pretenders stood a true magnate — one wealthy enough to bankroll a dozen prosperous merchants at once.
 
So the wardens followed every lead, tracing financial channels in search of the true Benefactor. But they found nothing — no records of large transfers, no sign of hidden accounts. The merchants they'd seized came from every walk of life: different trades, origins, ages, genders, even quirks of personality. Their only common ground was this: each had found sudden success in recent years, and each commanded considerable wealth. Every one of them swore the funds used to support Forsaken operations came from their own trade — and all, with striking unanimity, claimed they had adopted the name "Benefactor" out of discontent with the Empire's oppression of the Charon. It was all too familiar. Just as Forsaken criminals ignored the law but never broke their own code, so too must these merchants have been lured by profit — or threatened into compliance — to act in such perfect unison.
 
The wardens reached a chilling conclusion: however the true Benefactor passed their money to these seemingly law-abiding merchants, they must possess insight beyond ordinary men — and a hand ruthless enough to enforce obedience. How many such merchants might already dance to their tune was impossible to say. If the merchants were fishermen chasing the tides along the shore, then the Benefactor was the one who commanded the sea itself. A trace of fear crept into the wardens' hearts. Perhaps this Benefactor truly stood at some higher vantage — and perhaps their very investigation was already unfolding in the palm of their hand.
 
Yet for most ordinary folk, the details scarcely matter. They know only this: that within the Forsakens is a leader known as the Benefactor — one of Atlasia's three great magnates, spoken of in the same breath as Ms Zhiliu of Huaxu and Lord Generous, one of the Seven Virtues of Elysium. Tavern chatter delights in speculation: how many zeroes trail the sum of their fortune; how many roast turkeys and lambs vanish at their table in a single feast; whether the candles in their manor ever need be blown out to save on lamp oil... And for those at the end of their rope, one last hope remains: that when they wake from their dreams, a letter from the Benefactor will be waiting before them.

name: Betwixt Leaves and Branches
desc: The following is drawn from the writings of Comnena, a scholar of Aethyrie. Her histories are notoriously abstruse, diverging in places from the official records of the Hyperborean Empire — and thus seldom seen beyond the shelves of collectors. Indeed, such tomes are more often purchased as ornament than for study; a single set may languish five years before leaving a bookseller's hand.

res.name: Betwixt Leaves and Branches: The Filthoid Waves
res.text:
Sacred Tower Era, Year 1–500: The Filthoid Waves
 
Long millennia past, the world was believed to consist of but two realms: in the south, the theocracy of Elysium; in the north, only untamed wilds. Elysium was a land consecrated to the Great Nine, where each community served its chosen deity. To the Patriarch the gods gave revelation, which was passed down through the ranks of the priesthood. These revelations, however, spoke only of reverence, awe, and piety — with little bearing on life, law, or anything of practical worth. In Elysium, life changed little from day to day. The Sacred Canon dictated when to rise, when to labour, when to take meals, and when to kneel in prayer and confession at the halls of praise. The faithful believed that when their time came, they would ascend to the Heaven above Heavens — a realm where honey ran in rivers and even the air itself was sweet. To us it may seem a stagnant existence — yet to those of that age, it was both the best and only way to live. To remain within the Church's fold was life; to leave it was to embrace near-certain death.
 
At that time, Filthoids were the shared plight of all humankind.
 
These were no ordinary beasts, but creatures that came in hordes — possessed of strength and cunning beyond common animals, and a boundless hatred for mankind. Be they Solarian, countless though they were, or the horned but fewer-numbered Charon, none could stand alone against a Filthoid pack. In the south, the Great Nine bestowed their might upon the faithful of Elysium. Their divine power was forged into sacred relics, and whoso bore them served as a vessel of the gods' authority, spreading their grace across the land. Only the most virtuous and pure of heart were chosen to wield such relics. These champions gathered followers and smote the Filthoids, their deeds honoured with titles echoing the Seven Virtues.
 
Yet as the wars wore on, some of these paragons fell in battle — and amid the chaos of the front lines, there was neither time to return their relics to the Holy Capital, nor to perform the long rites of selection and investiture. So with centuries passing thus, the relics ceased to return to the Holy Capital, and were passed instead from bearer to bearer, guided by the will of the predecessors. These heirs became the first knight-commanders. Around them gathered retainers and the faithful alike, forming the first knightly orders.
 
In their wars against the Filthoids, each knightly order honed a style of war all their own. Commander Patience favoured the hammer-and-anvil. Clad in full plate, his heavy infantry would draw the Filthoid swarms upon themselves. While the beasts clawed in vain at walls of iron, the Commander led his cavalry forth from ambush — crashing in from all sides like a god's own hammer, to crush the foe between them. By contrast, the order of Generosity practised war with splendour. Their commander, an archer without peer, commanded the largest host of bowmen in Elysium. Before battle, he would seize a high ridge for his killing ground, arraying his archers in scattered bands to cover every angle. Their storm of arrows would break the Filthoids before they ever reached the lines — so that in the best of cases, the heavy infantry might win the day without spilling a drop of blood.
 
Through long years of war these tactics reached refinement, and the southern reaches of the continent were slowly drawn beneath the Church's dominion. Yet the shadow of failure never strayed far. In the five-hundredth year of the Sacred Tower Era, a horde rose greater than any before. As though guided by cunning, the Filthoids bypassed several knightly garrisons and drove straight for the Church's heart — the Holy Capital itself. By the time the orders grasped the threat, no hour remained to marshal stratagems or shape the field. They could only stand with mortal flesh against a countless swarm, fighting in chaos and desperation. Mankind's one advantage over the Filthoids lay in the discipline of ordered war. Once battle collapsed into primal struggle, the outcome could be nothing but tragedy. Midway through the clash, the orders of Loyalty and Humility were slain to the last — commanders and cohorts alike. Even the order of Diligence, famed for the might of its individual warriors, fared little better: their commander lost an arm to the beasts' onslaught. Just as the remaining knights steeled themselves to perish, resolved that no Filthoid would breach the high walls of the Holy Capital, a miracle was wrought. From the central spire of the city rose a perfect moon, which descended to the heart of the battlefield. Thus appeared the ninth of the Great Nine — the first to reveal divinity — the Goddess of the Full Moon and Fate. The Sacred Canon of Elysium speaks of many wonders, oft dismissed as embellishment. Yet the chronicles of this descent record marvels more astounding still — eclipsing even the Canon's own miracles.
 
The goddess raised her sacred right arm and pointed to the heavens. The sky split asunder, revealing its black foundation. With her finger she struck that dark vault ten times, and at each touch a light was kindled. At first no larger than a pinhole, the lights swelled — to the size of camels, then of hippos — until at last they plunged earthward. The roars of the falling lights surpassed the bellow of a hundred lions. Their blasts scorched like molten iron, driving before them clouds of poisoned dust. The Filthoids, driven to frenzy by the goddess's falling lights, burst apart — their forms shattered, their essence undone. Yet the faithful who fought in her name were bathed in that same radiance and felt not fire, but coolness. Though their eyes beheld a vision of hellfire, their skin knew only the touch of spring water — and in their hearts welled a rapture beyond measure. Such was the goddess's grace.
 
Thus was the second great crisis of the Elysian Church ended under the goddess's protection. In later ages, some would claim the chronicles of this miracle were pure invention. Yet the knights who endured the battle became zealots unshakable — vowing to spend their every drop of sweat and blood in defence of the Holy Capital. Fortunate indeed that never again did a Filthoid wave of such scale rise upon Elysian soil.
 
Yet across the continent lay lands untouched by divine gaze. At the Church's northernmost bounds stretched the Emerald Forest. Beyond it lay country unknown: not barren, but rich with plains and ample rain. But long harried by Filthoids, men knew well what awaited any who strayed beyond the gods' protection and the knights' guard: it was no different from exile into a perilous wilderness. A few fervent preachers, undaunted by death, ventured northward — but seldom returned whole. To the common folk of Elysium, daily life may have mirrored the pages of the Canon a little too closely, yet even tedium was preferable to death. Thus it was only dimly known that a vast land stretched beyond the north, equal in breadth to the Church's own dominion. Few gave thought to that Filthoid-haunted land — not until the Great Migration of Sacred Tower Year 998.

res.name: Betwixt Leaves and Branches: The Eve of Uprising
res.text:
Sacred Tower Era, Year 900–998: The Eve of Uprising
 
In Sacred Tower Year 998, a great uprising swept across the southern continent, shaking even the seemingly unshakable Elysian Church. Though the revolt failed to overthrow the Church, its remnants fled north — founding a succession of new realms. Together, these events became known as the Great Migration.
 
For a thousand years, the Church upheld its theocracy. From high priest to commoner, all believed this order eternal — shielding the world from the Filthoid threat beyond, and sustaining life within, day after day, until the end of time. Yet each new Filthoid wave, though deepening fear and strengthening the Church's authority, quietly set in motion changes that reshaped the land itself.
 
The Filthoid invasions placed different burdens upon each stratum of Elysian society.
 
Foremost among the burdened were the knightly orders, who suffered grievous losses in every Filthoid invasion. Yet after each war, they rebounded with startling speed. The valour of the knights — and the claim that they had seen gods with their own eyes — inspired the common folk. Thus the faithful flocked to join the orders. Most would never rise to knighthood, serving instead as common soldiers, yet they felt thereby closer to the divine, and some even yielded their lands willingly to the orders.
 
Thus the knightly orders — once purely martial — became institutions of military, economic, commercial, and even religious power. Their devotion to the Great Nine merged with personal loyalty to their commanders. From this fusion of faith and wealth emerged a new social force: the military nobility.
 
They were called nobility because the post of knight-commander — once granted by divine choice, election, or contest — began to pass by blood. Commanders' kin filled the orders' ranks, managing finances, land disputes, and rites. In the more arrogant orders, it's said their feasts even outshone ceremonies for the gods. At the time few thought this amiss — but later events proved the danger. For when reverence for a man outstrips reverence for the gods, that man holds power enough to cast them down.
 
Next came the plight of the freeholding farmers. Before the Filthoid invasions, most lived near towns in modest self-sufficiency. But war left many lands desolate. Those who lost their fields sought the protection of knight-commanders — becoming tenant farmers, bound to their estates. At the same time, rebuilding the ravaged regions gave rise to a new force: the merchant.
 
These merchants were no peddlers or wandering hawkers. They bought up the goods of entire regions, then sold them wholesale to lands under reconstruction. Their trade spanned vast distances — yet many never left their grand estates. All was moved by money alone, while the dispossessed farmers became mere cogs within their elaborate designs.
 
At first, these merchants still feared the Church's edicts, taking only what they deemed a rightful share. But in time, their sense of what was "rightful" grew warped — and their fortunes soared to staggering heights.
 
As these great magnates rose, the farmers' plight grew ever more dire. When a farmer stood before not just a merchant, but a knight-commander too, he bore a double yoke — of coin and of arms. In famine years — or even sooner — he might sell his land, fall into tenancy, and still be forced to offer tribute for knightly rites. Such lives were no longer bearable. Yet many clung to the belief that all was divine will... until a new thought stirred: Why would the gods ordain such misery for us?
 
And what of the gods' own servants? The clergy — those closest to divinity — remained secure in their sanctuaries, faithfully obeying oracles from the Holy Capital. In principle, they stood untouched by the turmoil — and in truth, most were. Yet some began to think otherwise. A few even joined the uprising and the Great Migration. Their numbers in the resistance were few — but their influence, profound.
 
At the root lay one question: What is divinity?
Is it a perfect being, who split its holiness into nine — becoming the Great Nine?
Or are the Nine each perfect — distinct, yet united in will, together forming the foundation of creation?
Were the Nine born in sequence? And if so, is one greater than the rest?
Above the gods... is there yet another god?
 
For centuries, such questions plagued Elysium's theologians. At last, in Sacred Tower Year 480, during the Eighth Universal Council, they reached a fragile consensus:
Divinity is manifold — its consciousness encompassing all things. It divided itself into nine, and so came the Great Nine: equal and one.
The divine is perfect, whole. All that occurs is its flawless design — both change and changelessness. For the divine is the immutable beyond change, the necessary beyond chance.
The divine is infinite, abiding at the beginning and end of time — the primal cause of all things.
 
The clergy debated for more than a century, forging a fragile accord. Yet just twenty years later, in Year 500, the Filthoid Waves shattered it.
 
The descent of the Goddess of the Full Moon and Fate proved divinity was real — yet also sparked new doubts: Were the Nine truly equal?
If all things are ordained by the divine... then were the Filthoid Waves too? And if so — why did the divine descend in person to end them?
 
Those already discontent with the Universal Councils' decrees found these questions echoing within. Their doubts mirrored the farmers': Could the gods truly be trusted?
As faith gave way to scepticism, some priests turned to old records — devising tests and studies to prove whether the divine existed at all.
 
The eight Universal Councils, once meant as pillars of doctrine, became weapons of dissent. The First was overturned by the Seventh; the Sixth absolved those condemned by the Second. Line after line of contradiction chipped away at the very idea of divine truth.
 
In response, the Church created a new role — the scholastic priests — tasked with quelling doubt and realigning thought. Over centuries, their efforts slowly brought unity back to the clergy. Yet a few remained fixated on old texts and speculative works, preferring ancient scrolls over new teachings. They were few, and the Church dismissed them as harmless cranks, lost in their books.
 
Among those few scholars stood a curious young priest named Alexis. He dreamed of writing a tome that answered every question — a book to mend the flaws in doctrine. To do so, he left the Holy Capital, journeying through the dioceses to see how the gods' grace truly moved among the people. He recorded all he saw.
 
But Alexis never returned. In time, he gained another name — the Sage. He joined with Dis Galea of the Three-Wolf Order, and together they led the uprising and opened a new chapter of history.

name: Investigation Notes on the Scourge of Zhuyin
desc: A survivor's early account of the Scourge of Zhuyin, told by a farmer from the mountain hamlets around Mistwharf.

res.text:
"Truth is, my whole world's no bigger than the patch of dirt in front of me. All that grand talk the gentry fuss over — who's right, who's wrong, what Lord Argent is up to — I can't make heads or tails of it. The High Chancellor of Loongyuan, the Outer Peaks folk, the Jishu Sect, the Xuanheng Sect... whoever they are, not one of them's ever made my crops grow an inch taller.
So before the Scourge of Zhuyin came, I'd never once imagined that the skinny lad we all called Scrap could be any kind of Drifter.
When the fields were quiet, I'd hear Old Wang ramble on about the people from the Outer Peaks — men with swords and wine gourds, hopping over rooftops like it was nothing, coming and going without a trace, living free as birds. Even if they didn't know any secret arts, they still looked the part: straight-backed, well turned out, just like the masters in the old stories.
But Scrap? All year round he's in the same torn vest, ragged shorts, and a beaten-up straw hat. From far off he looks more like a monkey than a boy. Come summer he's baked so dark he turns red. Not a single thing about him said "master" of any kind.
Who'd have thought that when those Sable Bi'an came tearing in, it'd be that scrawny scrap of a boy who'd end up saving our skins?
Those Bi'an came fast — too fast for us to burn a stick of incense or run begging to the gentry for help. People died; fields were ripped apart. Just when we thought it was the end for us, Scrap stepped forward with his hoe. Told me to get the others out. Said he was a Drifter from the Outer Peaks, and that he had to stand his ground and hold those beasts back.
I was scared half to death, so I did what he told me. But on the way down the path, I couldn't help looking back. Think of it — it might've been the only time in my life I'd ever see someone like the heroes in those old tales.
But what I saw wasn't some great hero in fine robes.
It was just a lad like us... Then a Bi'an knocked him flying — blood everywhere. Yet he dragged himself up by that hoe and hurled himself at them again. And again. Until every last one of us had run far enough that they couldn't see us anymore...
That's how it happened. So... do you know how to get word to the Outer Peaks? I want to take Scrap's bones back there, along with the letter he left behind. He's the one who saved my life. And he's the one who taught me this: a hero isn't made by the skills he's got — it's the brave, honest heart that counts..."

name: The Compendium of Verbal Stratagems
desc: A tattered, heavily scribbled-over volume. Its author seems to have recorded countless case studies meant to teach readers how to seize the upper hand in argument... yet now it lies abandoned, cast aside by someone.

res.text:
In Huaxu, one ought not rely on brute force — yet, as we all know, words can cut just as sharply.
Thus did I spend years roaming the land, observing every quarrel, retort, and petty squabble I could find, and distilled the entire art of human rhetoric into four supreme manoeuvres: LMAO, copypasta, bootlicking, and seething. Master these, and you shall never again lose ground in an argument.
Allow me to present a few examples. First, the proper deployment of LMAO...
 
(The rest of the pages have been brutally crossed out. You close the book, and on the back cover you find a single bold word scrawled across it: copypasta.)

name: Loong in the Sky
desc: A lazily titled serial novel. It follows a youth named Zhao Hao, who is chosen as the High Chancellor of Loongyuan. Wildly popular among Huaxu's young readers.

res.name: Loong in the Sky — Chapter Five
res.text:
Chapter Five — "The New High Chancellor"

"Useless wretch!"
The slap cracked through the hall like a whip. The boy reeled, clutching his cheek, his gaze darting sideways — and that timid look only made the old man before him tremble with even sharper fury.
"Our family has served in high office within the Xuanheng Sect for generations! And yet it produced you — a useless, good-for-nothing failure! After all the toil and sweat I spent raising you, is this what I'm repaid with? How are you meant to face our honoured forebears!?"
"Alright, Zhao — breathe."
A soft, feminine voice drifted from a bench in the corner. Its owner, robed in green, narrow-featured, a glimmer coiled deep behind the eyes, looked almost like a green serpent draped in human skin.
He set down his teacup and rose to stand behind the furious Zhao Yan.
"Qing Lan, don't bother talking sense into me. I'll beat this disappointing son of mine dead if I have to!"
"Zhao, spare us the tragic-father act. The young master's coming-of-age has passed, yet he's mediocre in study, weak in physique, plain in appearance — and he can't even manage the basic incense rites an incense warden must command. Everyone knows this. Even if you beat him to death here and now, it won't alter the Qing House's decision."
"I'm not—"
Smack.
Another slap landed hard across the boy's face.
"Quiet, you disgrace of a son!"
Zhao Yan bowed his head, dragging in several harsh breaths before forcing the words out between clenched teeth:
"Now that the Qings have spoken so plainly... there's nothing left to discuss."
"Naturally. Whatever the elders agreed upon years ago, our generation shapes matters to fit the present. And the present is this: the young master of the Zhao House is unfit for our lady — by every measure."
"Give us five years... no, three—"
Qing Lan released a long, weary sigh.
"You truly don't take a hint, do you? Forget it. The head of our house anticipated this outcome. Here — read it."
He drew a gilt-bound red letter from his sleeve and held it out.
"A... betrothal letter!?"
"The young heir of the Zhou family is but sixteen, yet already a reserve Court Memorial Envoy — brilliant, handsome. This is the will of the Qing House's master... and of the young lady herself."
"Zhou? That wretch... he used to trail after me like a little lapdog..."
"That was then. Circumstances change. I have conveyed the decision. I'll take my leave."
Qing Lan turned and made for the courtyard. Zhao Yan sagged in defeat, and his disappointing son remained bowed beside him, useless and silent. Just then — white mist burst across the Zhao estate.
"Wh—What's happening...?"
Soft bands of white light tore down through the clouds. No incense burned, and yet a rich, heady fragrance spilled into the courtyard.
Several Bi'an, treading upon iridescent clouds, descended from above. They passed the stunned Qing Lan, swept past the kneeling Zhao Yan — and halted before Zhao Hao. One by one, they laid the white blossoms held in their jaws into his open palm.
"This... this is impossible!!!"
Qing Lan's scream scraped from his throat — but it was swallowed beneath a vast voice surging through the mind of every witness, forcing upon them the words he least wished to hear:
"From this moment forth — by decree — Zhao Hao is appointed High Chancellor of Loongyuan."

name: The Collected Tales of Uncle Feng
desc: These fantastical tales are said to have been told by an old man called Uncle Feng. They proved so entertaining that later generations gathered them into a single book. Though some adults find certain passages a touch unsettling, the collection is still printed across Huaxu and remains dearly loved by children.

res.name: The Collected Tales of Uncle Feng (Excerpt)
res.text:
Now, in the days when the Nine Chapters of Dafenghad only just come into being, there stood a remote mountain village at Mistwharf. In it lived a herdboy. Orphaned at a young age, he spent his days tending a small flock of lambs. When he turned thirteen, his youngest lamb went missing. As forlorn as the little creature itself, the boy treasured it above all the rest — so he set out at once, following its tiny hoofprints.
But misfortune struck: the boy slipped and tumbled into a ravine. Half-conscious, he felt sweet dew touch his lips and warm dawnlight press against his eyelids. When he came to, he found a cluster of spirits beside him — shaped like dewdrops, gleaming with a glassy sheen — surely the beings known as the Wishen.
Seeing him stir, the Wishen squeaked in fright and scattered into the bushes, their heads and tails all in a fluster — a most comical sight. Only after some time did they creep back, each carrying a little cup rolled from leaves. They had gathered dew to save him.
"Was it you who saved me?"
Their little leader nodded shyly and held out the cup of dew.
The boy said, "Thank you for helping me. May I come along with you?"
The spirits gladly agreed. They picked wild fruit and gathered honey, using flowers as cups and leaves as plates, and they played with the boy all through the day in the forest.
From that day on, no one knew where the solitary boy had gone. Only from the white chrysanthemums on the mountainside would soft laughter drift out from time to time — so people say the boy and the Wishen are still living happily in a hidden fairy haven.

name: The Last Writings of an Unknown
desc: A notebook left by an unknown hand near Zhuyin Altar, its ink already blurred in places. It records in detail the ordeal its author faced here. None can know in what despair he set down these final words.

res.text:
It is said that north of Mistwharf, hidden within the mists of the inner sea, stands the Crouching-Loong Pillar, where a fiend named Zhuyin is said to lurk.
The baleful miasma that seeps across the lands of Huaxu is believed to rise from this very place. People shrink from its evil and dare not draw near. Yet if we quail and turn aside, how shall Huaxu ever regain its clear winds and broad, bright heavens? Thus I took leave of my family and, with fifteen able youths, set out for the Pillar to uncover the truth — hoping to be the first to lift the blight of Zhuyin.
Breaking through the thunderous mist, we reached the cliff and at last beheld it in full. Shaped like a pine, rising straight into the clouds, it is the Crouching-Loong Pillar — and the name is no falsehood. Circling it several times, we found a stone ledge where we could bring the boat ashore.
Jagged rocks lay everywhere, all dark as ink. For miles we saw no green. Cloud swirled; thunder did not cease. Truly, as the tales say, this was a place steeped in ill omen. The limbs of my companions trembled, some near to fleeing. Thus we sent back the three who were each their family's only son. The remaining thirteen pressed on.
After half a day's climb, a baleful beast rose from the mire — a creature in the shape of a Bi'an, its body wholly black — and descended upon us. Though sturdy and strong, my men could not match it. And though we lived under the Nine Chapters of Dafeng, even Lord Argent's protection could not reach us here; thus we took refuge within a cavern. Lin's firstborn, Jianchen, stepped before us and met his end — alas for him!
The higher we climbed, the keener the cold grew; no robe nor fur could fend it. Ten miles farther on, we reached a stone terrace ringed with steps raised over the very void. Looking up, we glimpsed a palace hanging upside down above the clouds, bound fast by more than ten chains of cold iron — an awe-striking sight. I fear it was a dwelling of the celestials, seized and fettered by the fiend.
Three days we remained there, fearful from dawn to dusk. Water and food were nearly spent, and the fiendish beasts hunted without rest. One youth, half-delirious, murmured that he had glimpsed a black loong surging through the gloom — its head and tail unseen — much like Taihao. The others sharply silenced him, saying that Taihao has guarded Huaxu for ages and must not be likened to some baleful shadow. Yet after much thought, I do not share their certainty.
Surveying the place, its layout seemed more a cage — and more still an altar. In youth I read widely, and learned that Huaxu holds the dual in highest regard: Heaven and Earth, yin and yang, clear and turbid. Thus, if there are two divinities, it would not be beyond reason.
We have been trapped here for more than half a month. The way back is lost; no path can be found. Only two of the youths remain. Thus I set down this record: should anyone find it, carry it to Haojing, and make known the truth to all our folk.

(The pages that follow appear to list the names of the party, but the writing is too worn to read.)

name: On Life and Death in Huaxu
desc: A cultural study by a foreign scholar examining Huaxu's distinctive understanding of life and death.

res.text:
In Huaxu, the Earthborn (the Solarian people) and the Loongscion (the Charon people) share a single doctrine concerning life and death — an occurrence of notable rarity. In most regions of the world, these two groups diverge, at least in part, in their beliefs. Even within Elysian, a theocratic state, there remain Charon who continue to uphold older traditions.

It is known that the forebears of Huaxu were originally Charon natives of this land, who later intermarried with migrants from the "Tower" that arrived around Year 1010 of the Sacred Tower Era. It is therefore reasonable to infer that the distinctive cultural unity now found in Huaxu has its roots in a shared aspiration toward harmonious coexistence.

People in Huaxu hold that upon death, one's soul proceeds to the Underworld, drinks from the waters of the River of Forgetting, severs all attachments to the present life, and is then reborn. This conception of unceasing renewal bears some resemblance to the Misty Sea traditions observed among the Charon people, yet it differs in one subtle respect: Huaxu doctrine appears to allow that the dead retain a measure of their own awareness.

According to Huaxu tradition, if the deceased continue to harbour attachments to the living world, they may defer rebirth and take on a form known as the Wishen, remaining among the living. This should not be conflated with the conventional "ghost" of fantasy literature; the concept is fundamentally distinct. Within Huaxu culture, Wishen are commonly portrayed as friendly, playful, and gentle beings who aid the living and engage with them in lighthearted ways, rather than instilling fear or causing harm.

name: Popular Characters in Huaxu Baby Names
desc: An unofficial overview of characters commonly used in Huaxu baby names in recent years, along with brief notes on their meanings. The sources are murky and the accuracy debatable — best approached as light reading, or simply for amusement.

res.text:
...

No. 24: Si
The character Si encompasses both reflective thought and quiet longing. It combines readily with other naming elements to express particular aspirations — for instance, Siyan ("thoughtful words"), Sigui ("yearning to return"), or Jingsi ("quiet contemplation"). It is also a frequent choice in generational names.

...

No. 11: Feng
Feng, the same character appearing in the Nine Chapters of Dafeng, carries a dignified, commanding air and traditionally reflects parents' hopes for future achievement. In recent years, however, younger parents have favoured it for its literal meaning — "wind" — wishing their child might grow freely, like a passing breeze.

...

No. 5: Yu
Yu, meaning "jade," evokes an image of a child cherished like the stone itself — gentle, refined, and precious. In Huaxu prosody, Yu is not a level-tone syllable, so pairing it with a level-tone character gives the name a smoother, more harmonious sound.

...

No. 1: Liu
Liu draws on imagery of flowing water and carries a calm, philosophical resonance. It appears in several classical Huaxu expressions originally featuring the character Liu — such as "enduring as a long river" and "following what is good as naturally as water flows". It has long been a well-loved character, but its recent surge owes much to Zhiliu, the current High Chancellor of Loongyuan. Since her appointment, not only has Liu risen sharply in popularity, but several visually similar Huaxu-script characters have also seen a remarkable uptick in use.
