name: Rites of Incense Offering
desc: Compiled by officials of Xuanheng Sect, this manual sets out the proper procedures for the incense-offering rite at the Argent Loong Temple.

res.text:
Rite of Divine Veneration

The Argent Incense joins Heaven, Earth, mortals, and the divine, bearing the grace bestowed by Lord Argent. Through its rising smoke, we offer our reverence.
Lord Argent is all-seeing and cares not for the number of sticks; sincerity alone reaches the divine. Worshipers may receive three offering sticks each day from the shrine.

When offering incense, observe the following essentials:
1. Purity of Body and Mind
Before the rite, attire shall be proper, and both body and mind kept clean and composed.
2. Proper Kindling
Hold the incense with the tips downward to take flame. Once all three sticks are fully kindled, take them properly in hand.
3. Correct Bearing
With the incense burning, hold it in both hands and stand upright with your head slightly bowed. The tips shall remain level and must never be directed towards another person.
4. The Three Reverent Bows
• First Bow: Before the holy image of Lord Argent, bow with head lowered — in reverence for the Nine Chapters of Dafeng, which uphold order.
• Second Bow: Bow again — in reverence to Lord Argent, whose grace reaches all living beings.
• Third Bow: Bow once more — in reverence to Bi'an, the divine beast who discerns right from wrong.
When the rite is complete, set the sticks upright in the censer, then withdraw with measured, reverent steps.

Incense is offered not for protection alone, but also in gratitude for divine grace. In our daily conduct, we shall uphold the precepts of the Nine Chapters of Dafeng and cultivate virtue — for therein lies true reverence.

name: Luoxiang's Case Notes
desc: One volume from Luoxiang's Case Notes. As a community mediator, Luoxiang applies her understanding of the Nine Chapters of Dafeng to everyday disputes, collecting her experiences into this series. Down-to-earth and practical, it has unexpectedly become a popular household read.

res.name: Luoxiang's Case Notes — Vol. 10
res.text:
...
Case Ten — A Nuisance Neighbour, Settled with The Compendium of Verbal Stratagems

A few years back, a man named Zhao Da came to me with a complaint. His new neighbour, Zhang San, had been pounding on his door before dawn each day, insisting that Zhao had "sung at midnight and wouldn't let him sleep". I'd known Zhao Da for years. He hauls cargo on the docks all day; the moment he gets home, he's out cold. The man sleeps like a stone — midnight singing wasn't even remotely possible. But Zhang San stuck to his story. Each day he came earlier, and louder. At last, one dawn when Zhao stumbled out half-asleep and thoroughly fed up, he opened the door and threw a punch. The Nine Chapters of Dafeng say: "Heaven's great virtue bears the name of Life; To wound or kill — this must not be done." By the code, Zhao Da had to be punished.
 Still, Zhang San had started the trouble, and that had to be dealt with as well. Reasoning proved useless, and brawling was out of the question. So I lent Zhao a book a friend once gave me — The Compendium of Verbal Stratagems — and told him to study it. The next morning, Zhang arrived as usual, shouting. Zhao simply stood inside the threshold and replied with the book's four stock phrases: "LMAO", "Copypasta", "Bootlicking", and "Seething". Within moments, Zhang was shaking with rage and actually raised a fist to strike — and Zhao quietly pulled back his sleeve, showing the fresh welt from his punishment the day before. Zhang froze, went pale, and backed away. He came again the next morning. Zhao answered in exactly the same way. After a few days of this, Zhang San stopped coming altogether.

name: Footsteps Across Huaxu
desc: This piece is part of Xu Xingke's Footsteps collection. Commissioned by Huaxu's local council, the renowned travel writer records his reflections on the many regions of his homeland.

res.name: Footsteps Across Huaxu — Mistwharf
res.text:
Mistwharf
 Step off the boat, and the first thing you'll see is Mistwharf. For the people of Huaxu, this stretch of land runs long — from Starwharf in the south to the Gritblight Expanse in the north.

Starwharf
When I meet visitors arriving in Huaxu for the first time, I always tell them not to rush inland. Linger on the quay a moment: hawkers call without pause, hardworking Huaxu porters haul crates from river barges, and Starweavers trade stories with friends from distant lands. There are few places more full of life.

EverSpring
Near the roots of the great tree lies EverSpring — another stop not to be missed. In Huaxu, everyone knows what the name stands for: to the Starweavers, it is the realm's largest guild; to visitors, a trove of rare and wondrous wares. Even if you plan to buy nothing, the towering statue of Lord Argent at the gate alone is worth the journey.

Twilight Ravine
 Few from Huaxu ever venture here. Set deep within the wilderness, the Twilight Ravine is said to be the resting place of Wishen — beings other lands might call "ghosts". These gentle spirits are best left undisturbed.
As a child, I once lost my way here and stumbled upon a vast pagoda tree, its gnarled branches aglow with a soft light. I followed the shimmer to a small island at the heart of a lake, where unfamiliar voices gently led me back to the path. Looking back now, that faint glimmer must have been the Spring of Yu, hidden deep within the Ravine.

Hall of Ephemerality
The Hall of Ephemerality is Fu family's ancestral hall of healing, devoted for generations to the Zhuyou method. Should you fall ill while travelling here, this is the place to seek aid. The healer cherishes silence: whether you come for treatment or merely pass through the apricot grove beyond, please keep your voice low, that her quietude may remain undisturbed.

Crowsong Hollow
When I was little, my parents would tell me the tale of the Battle of Shuli at bedtime — how the Xuanheng Sect and the Jishu clashed upon this plain, leaving not a soul standing. But when I asked what they had fought for, they never had an answer.
Now, under Taihao's protection, Huaxu has known peace for generations. The rusted remnants of Mechapuppets lie scattered across the plain, worn by wind and time — a silent draw for scholars from far and wide.

res.name: Footsteps Across Huaxu – Haojing
res.desc: An excerpt from Xu Xingke's Footsteps Across Huaxu, an officially commissioned travelogue. In it, Xu sets down his impressions of his homeland — its regions, its people, and the ideas they awaken.
res.text:
Hall of Adjudication

In the early days of the Nine Chapters of Dafeng, the Hall of Adjudication played a far more prominent role. Its original purpose, however, has long since faded from common memory and is now known only to a handful of dedicated historians.

Beneath the Hall, a bridge-like span arches across the air like a rainbow. Legend holds that Lord Argent sometimes soars through the heavens and listens, unmoving, to the clamour of the mortal world — proof that Heaven heeds the people, and that divine law watches over all.

Today, the Hall stands as Huaxu's political centre. It rises against the clouds, visible from nearly anywhere in Haojing — much as the Nine Chapters of Dafeng stand before the people: clear, enduring, and impossible to ignore.

⸻

Zesheng Pharmacy

In former times, the people of Huaxu turned to healers of the Zhuyou clan when illness struck. In later ages, physicians devoted to pharmacology emerged, along with apothecaries to prepare and dispense medicines.

Zesheng Pharmacy is Haojing's most respected establishment of its kind. It is said that its founder was once herself a Zhuyou, yet she abandoned those arts in favour of pharmacology, elevating the discipline to new heights. Rare herbs and medicinal ingredients are supplied here, and the pharmacy is renowned for its proprietary prescriptions. It also offers seasonal wellness regimens to help preserve one's health.

If thirst overtakes you while wandering the streets, do stop by — herbal tonics are served free to the public.

⸻

Youlai Alley

Some popular Huaxu tales claim that the dead may linger in a form known as Wishen. Unlike the fearful portrayals of spirits and ghosts found in other lands, Huaxu's Wishen are remembered in legend as gentle, even endearing beings. Though they may occasionally cause minor disturbances, it is often out of kindness, as if to guide the living along their path.

Haojing folklore speaks of a place called Youlai Alley, where Wishen with unfinished attachments are said to gather. Most dismiss such claims as idle fancy. Yet there are whispers that if one follows the winding lanes of the eastern quarter long enough, one might, by chance, stumble into that mysterious domain...

⸻

Jiaolan Village

If Haojing's bustle begins to wear on you, head west. Jiaolan Village offers a quiet refuge from the city's noise. This small settlement lies on Haojing's western outskirts, close enough to reach on foot.

Huaxu's incense culture stretches back into antiquity, and Jiaolan Village is regarded as its birthplace. Though the craft of incense-making has long since spread across the land, and Jiaolan is no longer the only place to find it, it remains home to the largest incense-drying grounds in the region surrounding Haojing. When the aromatic plants come into bloom, villagers harvest them, rinse them clean, and lay them out beneath the sun. On fair days, when a gentle breeze passes through, the fragrance carries for miles, creating an atmosphere at once ethereal and intoxicating.

Before you depart, should you wish to bring home a thoughtful gift, the villagers' handcrafted incense makes an excellent choice: elegant in scent, and rich in Huaxu's distinctive cultural character.

name: Chronicles of the Starweavers
desc: Penned by the Starweavers themselves, this chronicle records the lives of their members in biographical form. As years pass and generations come and go, the task is taken up anew by each successor.

res.text:
[Ju]

The Starweavers trace their origins to Ju — the wise sovereign who first founded Huaxu.

In the wake of establishing the Jishu Sect, Ju journeyed south to the Sacred Tower in search of a means to avert calamity. Upon his return, he brought with him those wearied by war, and together they set about restoring their homeland. In those days, the land was in need of renewal on every front. To supply what each province lacked, folk began to trade across the realm — and so began the craft that would one day define the Starweavers.

Today, trade routes span the breadth of the continent, and wherever such paths may lead, the Starweavers are found. We cross mountains and rivers, travelling far beyond borders — not in pursuit of profit alone, but to bind together the many threads of civilisation. For wherever a merchant treads, there too travel the craft of the artisan and the learning of distant lands. From the meeting of these sparks, the flame of human endeavour endures.

...

name: Greenwich Archaeological Society — Project Applications
desc: A compiled record of project proposals submitted by members of the Greenwich Archaeological Society, each annotated with handwritten directives from Mr Qiu.

res.text:
[ID] L-W-01384
Subsea Investigation of the Luca Temple Complex
[Project Summary]
This project proposes an investigation of the trench west of the Luca Isles, commonly referred to as Andimin's Broken String. Recent, credible intelligence suggests the presence of an extensive architectural complex at considerable depth — a discovery of great significance, given that no known technology currently permits large-scale construction more than 500 metres beneath the sea. Such a finding calls into question the long-held belief that the Luca artists' reverence for a subsea deity was mere fevered fancy; their object of worship may, in fact, have had a material foundation. Despite the severe technical challenges posed by current diving limitations, we seek authorisation to conduct a preliminary survey. A successful probe may yield vital evidence concerning Luca religious practice and clarify its connection to the region's distinctive artistic tradition.
[Schedule]
Early March to late June (scheduled to avoid the king-tide period)
[Budget]
1.217 million silver coins (see appendix)
[Decision]
Approved.
Comments:
1. Ensure all personnel carry Mind-Purifying Powder and submit them for regular cross-checks to confirm continued mental stability.
2. Keep all storage rooms properly dehumidified. I have no desire to find yet another room reeking of mould.

[ID] A-C-02577
Excavation of a Burial Site from the Great Migration
[Project Summary]
Recent engagements between the Empire's 8th Legion and Aethyrie resistance forces have uncovered an unrecorded ancient burial site. Preliminary assessment by local personnel suggests that the remains likely belonged to resistance fighters who fell during the Great Migration. Although all textiles and paper artefacts have deteriorated beyond recovery, osteological analysis and the surviving metal objects are expected to yield information of academic value.
[Schedule]
Immediate deployment recommended; estimated duration approximately two months.
[Budget]
104,000 silver coins (see appendix)
[Decision]
Approved.
Comments:
1. Select personnel capable of handling combat if necessary. If additional protection is required, increase the budget and hire external security.
2. Coordinate with Arcadia Academy for conservation and identification work. Finalise arrangements with them directly.

[ID] H-N-03474
Historical Verification of the Founding of Hyperborea
[Project Summary]
The Icelake region in Hyperborea is approaching its annual thaw, creating an optimal window for lake-bed investigation. With newly acquired underwater survey equipment, the Society is now equipped to examine areas that were previously inaccessible.
[Schedule]
June to August
[Budget]
129,000 silver coins (see appendix)
[Decision]
Postponed.
Comments:
The Hyperborean Empire remains unstable, and the Forsakens appear to be preparing another strike that may reach Icelake. Do not proceed until the area is secure.

name: Lunocarp's Trade Tricks & Tips
desc: A pocket notebook Lunocarp keeps close at all times — now in its seventh volume. Inside are bursts of inspiration, scribbled down whenever they strike, whether in a sudden spark or after long deliberation. And in these newest pages, the influence of her latest muse is unmistakable: Snow the "Demon King", a traveller from far-off Hyperborea.

res.name: Lunocarp's Trade Tricks & Tips – Vol. VII
res.text:
...

※ Blind Draw
Put each item into one of my specially made Lucky Eggs — they all look exactly the same. Customers won't know what's inside until they pick one and crack it open. They say it makes shopping far more exciting — and the thrill of landing something rare is twice as sweet.
What if someone gets too lucky? Even better! That just makes them want to draw again... and again!
And their big win makes great word-of-mouth — the kind that draws in even more curious customers. Either way, Lunocarp can't lose!

※ Guaranteed Prize
Make sure that after a customer opens a certain number of Lucky Eggs, they're guaranteed to get at least one rare. Sounds like a loss, right? Not at all — it puts them at ease. They'll think, "Worst case, I'll just buy enough Eggs to hit the guarantee."
 And on their way there? They almost always open a few extras without even realising it!

※ Limited-Time Offer
For a short, special window, sell Lucky Eggs that might contain a particular item. Once that "miss it and it's gone" feeling kicks in, customers will scramble to buy as many as they can!

※ Partnered Prizes / Collab Prizes
Team up with someone influential and release a special prize together. Their fans will come running to buy my Lucky Eggs too — sales will soar!
And if I throw in a Limited-Time Offer on top of that? Boom — even greater impact!
As for my very first collab... of course it has to be with the Demon King from Hyperborea! It'll sell like hotcakes!

name: Notice: External Trade Temporarily Suspended
desc: A brief formal directive issued by EverSpring.

res.text:
To all residents of Mistwharf:

In light of the Scourge of Zhuyin, contamination within the Gritblight Expanse continues to intensify and is now spreading outward. Sable Bi'an have been frequently sighted in the surrounding regions and pose a grave threat to public safety. Effective immediately, EverSpring will suspend all overland trade from Mistwharf to the interior that passes through designated high-risk zones.

This measure has been submitted to the Ministry of Fortune for approval. All residents are required to comply with this directive and must not endanger their lives in pursuit of trivial profit.

For enquiries or unresolved matters, please contact EverSpring.

name: A Letter from One Starweaver to Another
desc: A letter addressed to the leader of a Huaxu trade caravan, apparently written by one of his former students.

res.text:
Mr Lin,

Thank you for your letter, especially amidst your many responsibilities. I am keeping well. Though I can no longer journey by sea, the work of handling goods still grants me faint glimpses of distant tales — a small comfort, but a comfort nonetheless. The ornaments you brought back from Luca are most intriguing. I shall examine them carefully and seek out suitable buyers.

My mother's condition has shown no improvement, and my two children are still very young. I cannot, in good conscience, leave the household entirely in my wife's care, and so I must once again decline your generous invitation. During my years with the caravan, you offered me much guidance; even after I left, you continued to welcome me back with the same kindness. I remain deeply grateful — and cannot help feeling a measure of shame for having disappointed you so often. May your journey be smooth, and may fortune grant you auspicious encounters along the way.

I have one further request: if your route happens to pass through Icelake in Hyperborea, please convey my regards to a young Loongscion woman named Jessica. She is about my younger sister's age, and should now be in her finest years. We became acquainted when our caravan last visited the city, and our parting was not an easy one. I had hoped we might meet again before long, yet the years have slipped quietly by. If you would be willing to deliver a few small gifts to her as an apology, I would be most grateful.
 
 With my warmest wishes for your health and peace,
 Jiayan

name: Where the Wicked Reign
desc: A memoir in Mr Qiu's own voice, chronicling how he shaped the black market into its present form.

res.name: Where the Wicked Reign — Ⅰ
res.text:
Rotten — down to the marrow.
That was the first thought that struck me the day I stepped into the black market, decades ago.
 Wreckage, refuse, and collapsed masonry lay strewn across the western shore. The air reeked of rot and the acrid burn of cheap incense. From the rubble's shadow, cold, hollow eyes watched the lone outsider in their midst — me.
Their gaze pleased me more than I cared to admit. In it, I glimpsed a hunger that mirrored my own.
They were the castoffs the Nine Chapters of Dafeng could never tame — refuse long abandoned by the world, shrinking from the sun and clinging to the shade. Some had lost an arm, others a leg — each bearing the wounds Bi'an leaves upon those who defy the Admonitions. Yet their eyes still tracked every newcomer with ravenous patience, lying in wait for the moment the unwary drifted too close — ready to wring out every last scrap of worth to survive another dawn, no matter how dear the cost.
Splendid. Truly splendid. No words of praise could ever do justice to such a place — a paradise pulsing with its own savage rhythm.
And I was quietly pleased.
For all the Nine Chapters' long schooling, each era preserves a gratifying number who never relinquish the one quality that matters most.
Greed — or, if you insist on a more civilised term, desire. So long as that primal instinct endures, even ants may strip an elephant to the bone.
With a little tending, this soil — so dense with desire — would bear a forbidden fruit Huaxu could not afford to ignore.
I doubt there is a sweeter satisfaction.

res.name: Where the Wicked Reign — Ⅱ
res.text:
Securing materials, outfitting the shopfronts, bringing merchants to heel — these initial steps in quickening the market required little effort on my part. Such matters, after all, are easily settled with coin.
The true work lay in the second step: cultivating recognition. Without that, nothing stands — nothing built on shifting sand ever does.
We had to teach people that the black market was no furtive haven for stolen goods and contraband, but — in their minds — the very emblem of possibility.
What others sold, we sold.
What others dared not, we sold — and openly.
Rarities and exotic beasts. Paintings and private hoards. Weapons, armaments, secrets, intelligence — even lives.
The Nine Chapters, in the end, are an ageing relic — a code concerned only with what must not be done. Turn it on its head, and all that lies unspoken becomes permissible: a broad freedom upon which the market could flourish.
Consider an example. Some hatreds end only in blood. A clean settling of scores invites Bi'an's censure. And yet... a hired hand? A carefully engineered ruin? The slow, social suffocation of a life?
The market need not take every commission, nor do I urge anyone to twist the code to their advantage. The point is simple: for a price, we offer a path towards long-cherished desires — and that is what wins the world's recognition of our reach.
Some will deem it wrong — even evil. Yet without evil, virtue has no meaning. Such is the creed my people of the market claim as their own.
Once those two steps were set in place, vitality followed of its own accord. From that moment, the market began, at last, to move along its rightful course.

res.name: Where the Wicked Reign — Ⅲ
res.text:
I once read of the so-called "Rule of One Hundred and Fifty": that beyond this number, friction multiplies and cooperation begins to decay.
The market crossed that threshold by its third year. From that point on, recognition alone no longer sufficed; an iron rule was required.
 Unlike my other ventures, the market keeps but a single law:
Those who place a wager must accept its result.
Trade here, and you gain the leverage to contend with those above you. Stand loyal to me, and the fetters of want fall away. Only one boundary limits privilege: take no pride in victory, and voice no complaint in defeat.
I turn a blind eye to profit that strays beyond conventional morality — but whoever pursues it must shoulder the risks as well.
As for those unequal to loss — at best: reclamation of assets, expulsion from the market, the withdrawal of shelter. At worst... such matters need not be set down in a memoir; I would not burden Huaxu's children with unwholesome dreams.

The essence of our rise has been spoken. What follows may serve merely as after-dinner anecdotes.

res.name: Where the Wicked Reign — Ⅳ
res.text:
The black market has never been a cage without exit. Over the decades, there were always those who chose to leave and pursue another path.
 Such intent has always pleased me; it affirms that my long-standing counsel has taken root: follow your desire.
To see them through that first and hardest step, I provided capital, manpower, and the necessary connections. Where desire is pursued, no investment is ever wasted.
Some did fail. Yet so long as the desire driving them did not wither, the market's favour remained with them.
Some succeeded, found their footing across various trades, and returned a portion of their gains to the market.
I ask no return; their offerings often hold little weight for me. But long distances are made of small steps, and even a modest force, rightly placed, may turn the course at a crucial moment.
Thus, through these ties, the market's branches spread through every quarter of Huaxu.
The sapling I planted has, under many hands, grown into a great tree — beyond any hope of uprooting.

name: Alchemist's Journal
desc: A journal left behind in Glevum Pit. The tone suggests it might belong to a scholar.

res.name: Alchemist's Journal (Ⅰ)
res.text:
Alchemist's Journal (Ⅰ)

(A journal left behind in Glevum Pit. The tone suggests it might belong to a scholar.)
...
April 16
We've found a peculiar <H>yellow crystal cluster</> in this pit. Judging by its texture, it's neither the legendary Crystallo of Stella said to be hidden deep in mountain caves, nor the Phoxene left behind in Glevum Pit. Instead, it appears to be a completely new, undiscovered mineral.
...
April 18
Bob was astonished to find that these yellow crystal clusters, which emitted a dim glow, had <H>grown larger</>. They had expanded from the size of a palm to that of a low shrub.
...
April 20
...The yellow crystal clusters had again "grown larger" and turned into spiky crystals that blocked our way, as if they were alive. Fortunately, they were fragile and could be easily broken with a small amount of <H>gunpowder</>.
Bob hypothesized that these crystals were not minerals but some kind of secretion from Filthoids — even a "subordinate form" of it. Over time, they expanded like a sponge soaked in water. Although Bob was well-versed in the Biology of Filthoids, this was still a bold assumption.
...
April 21
To verify Bob's hypothesis, we decided to venture deeper into the pit. If his guess is right, there must be a special Filthoid <H>parent form</> down there, different from the ones we've seen in the wild.
...

res.name: Alchemist's Journal (Ⅱ)
res.desc: A journal left behind in Glevum Pit, stained dark red. The handwriting matches the earlier journal found. The latter part is extremely messy, as if it was scribbled in frantic haste.
res.text:
Alchemist's Journal (Ⅱ)

(A journal left behind in Glevum Pit, stained dark red. The handwriting matches the earlier journal found. The latter part is extremely messy, as if it was scribbled in frantic haste.)

...
April 23
As Bob predicted, we found that special Filthoid deep in the pit, an area once deemed the "Forbidden Zone" of Glevum Pit.
It measures over 20 meters in length, making it the largest Filthoid I've ever encountered. It resembles a skeleton, with yellow crystals continuously "growing" from the ends of its limbs—we can be certain that it is the "parent form" of the yellow crystals we've seen along the way.
We've decided to stay hidden and continue observing this creature.
...
April 26
We've found that, compared to other wandering Filthoids, this one has a distinct peculiarity in addition to its larger size: It seems to have a particular fascination with <H>glowing minerals</>. It often wanders to abandoned mining pits, repeatedly performing the same digging motions. Whenever it unearths glowing minerals—such as Phoxene fragments from the mines or the Silverite from the mountains—it grows yellow crystals from the tips of its limbs to encase these luminous rocks.
Bob is extremely intrigued by this habit: Its behavior of excavating, collecting, and encapsulating the glowing objects doesn't seem to be a mere phototaxis. This series of actions appears to be something more akin to "conscious" behavior.
Is it possible that Filthoids retain some form of consciousness similar to that of humans? If this hypothesis is proven to be true, it would completely overturn the existing research findings in the field of the Biology of Filthoids.
...
April 27
We made a grave mistake.
In an attempt to further verify its behavioral patterns, Bob tried to provoke it by stealing from its "collection" and observing its reaction.
However, we severely underestimated its reaction speed. It lunged at us with a speed we had never witnessed before, attempting to tear us, the unwelcome intruders, into pieces.
Though Bob bought me enough time to escape its lair, I knew all too well that the injuries I had sustained were fatal. I would never make it out of this abandoned mine alive.
If anyone finds this journal, I implore you to take it to The Spathatoi Academy in Dismania. The study of this Filthoid—whom we named "the Crystalophile"—could bring about a monumental shift in the Biology of Filthoids as we know it.
Knowledge should not be buried with us in this pit.

Ines Morley, an Alchemist

name: A Lost Sheet – Mistwharf
desc: A collection of enigmatic pages discovered by chance. Some are delicate scrolls of fine parchment; others, freshly printed sheets with ink still crisp and dark. A few are no more than torn scraps from half-used notebooks. Whether neatly penned or barely legible, they all share one thing in common — each contains a hint pointing to the whereabouts of a hidden treasure.

res.name: Mistwharf (Ⅰ)
res.text:
Ughh... A few days ago, trying to show off in front of my friends, I climbed all the way up onto the head of the Bi'an statue <H>behind the Admonition Stele</>. Now I've come down with a cold and taken a nasty fall. Feels like punishment catching up with me...
I've left all of this month's pocket money at <H>Lord Bi'an's feet</>. Really hope Lord Bi'an won't hold it against me...

res.name: Mistwharf (Ⅱ)
res.text:
...

21 September
I felt like trying my luck today, so I opened five Lucky Eggs. The first four were nothing special: a box of toothpicks, a rag, a packet of Skylily seeds, and some throat lozenges. But the last one actually turned out to be a packet of fine Mistwharf Green Tea!
 Lunocarp said my luck was pretty good... could I really be Lady Luck's favourite after all!?
 Might try a few more when I get the chance.

...

27 September
Opened ten Lucky Eggs today. Got three sachets, a voucher for osmanthus cakes, two discount coupons that each take seven silver off a better theatre seat (and they don't even stack!), a wooden brush, a hundred grams of dried peafowl droppings — the note says it's medicinal, but it's honestly just disgusting, so I'll probably bury it in the field when I get home — plus a block of ink and a box of matches.
 Darn it... not a single rare item these past few days! If it weren't for how cute Lunocarp is, I really wouldn't bother opening another one.

28 September
Lunocarp talked me into opening more than twenty Lucky Eggs today. She said I'd hit the guarantee and could get a "super rare" one. And what was inside? Two slips of paper, pet food, and some kid stuff!!!
What a rip-off! Why doesn't Bi'an step in and do something about it!?
I'm done. I'm never opening another Lucky Egg again!

In a minute I'm throwing the rubbish straight into the <H>lotus pond</> to feed the fish!

res.name: Mistwharf (Ⅲ)
res.text:
I am but an old wanderer of the Wuqiongzang Sect. By chance I came upon this quiet, hidden place and made it my training ground.
Now, having lived more than seventy years, it is time for these old bones to retire from the martial world. You who have found this note — to reach this place, you must possess uncommon aptitude and no small measure of courage.
I have buried a treasured martial manual <H>beneath the apricot tree in the rear court of the Hall of Ephemerality</>.
Follow its teachings, and within half a month you will cross water without leaving a trace; train for a further half-month, and a thousand miles will be but a single day's journey to you.

I leave this manual to you now. May it carry you swiftly towards the peak of your art.

res.name: Mistwharf (Ⅳ)
res.text:
Ever since our debate that day, one thing has become clear to me: if we stay in Haze Market, we will never know what freedom truly is, nor what it costs.

What we do here — all the little tricks and the loopholes we exploit — are merely ways of bending the rules without ever going beyond them. I don't want freedom that lives on compromise. There must be a freedom in this world that needs no cunning and no pretence... and I want to prove it exists. So I have to go — beyond the mountain we've looked to so many times, and further still, to heights neither of us has yet seen. Even if it means becoming a wanderer, cut loose from the world.

By the time you read this, I will be far away. I've left a few gifts <H>on the old boat by the water</> where we always played. Forgive me for leaving without a proper farewell, but I promise you this: we will meet again, on the day I find my answer.

res.name: Mistwharf (Ⅴ)
res.text:
I'd heard the Gritblight Expanse was brutally dangerous, and after today's wandering... well, it really is — terrifying at times, but thrilling all the same. Look closely and the place even has a strange sort of beauty to it; if not for the Filthoids running wild, it might pass for a scenic spot.

But with nothing around me except rock and deadwood, it's far too easy to lose your bearings. I left a pack behind earlier when I stopped to rest — I'm fairly sure it was in some <H>cave</>... but after circling the area for ages, I still can't find the entrance. At this rate, night will catch me out here.

Forget it. Whoever comes across it can have it...

name: An Admonishing Note
desc: A handwritten note, its bold and forceful strokes carrying the unmistakable severity of an older hand.

res.text:
Wake up, young man. Keep your feet on solid ground. There is no such thing as gaining without graft. Every master of the Wuqiongzang Sect earned their skill through years of hard, honest training, and nothing else.
 
Stop swallowing nonsense like Loong in the Sky; that trashy tale has led enough gullible lads astray. Don't fool yourself into thinking fortune will drop into your lap and carry you to the top with no effort of your own.
 
Take this small sum and get yourself looked at. A fall from a cliff is no small matter. From now on, train steadily. Keep your head clear. Stop daydreaming, and stop chasing shortcuts that lead nowhere!

name: On Incense Offerings: Observances of Sacrifice
desc: A treatise that appears to set down the rites governing Huaxu's Grand Incense Rite. It enumerates the sacrificial observances of antiquity in meticulous detail and concludes with marginal notes left by an unidentified hand.

res.text:
Prepare a red calf; burn it to the south, in sacrifice unto High Heaven.
Take sheep and swine, and bury them to the north, in sacrifice unto the Bounteous Earth.
To the east, offer unto the Sun; to the west, unto the Moon.
Establish the pit and altar, and offer separate rites to the Four Quarters and the Four Seasons.
At the time of sacrifice, the Three Masters of Rites shall officiate.
Whoso Taihao favours shall bear the Lunarose Incense and stand at the centre, to make offering unto the Divine Lord.
Whoso is broadly learned shall bear the Sumei Incense and stand to the left, to make offering unto the ancestors.
Whoso excels in the myriad arts shall bear the Aurumwood Incense and stand to the right, to make offering unto the Spirits of Land and Grain.
Let no garments be adorned with deep indigo or dark crimson; let neither red nor purple be worn as inner raiment.
Speak not during the rite. When the offerings are complete, keep watch over the sacrificial fire for the space of a quarter-hour.
Let sacrificial food not be kept overnight; should it be kept beyond three days, it shall not be used.

Note: These regulations are intricate and lavish, and do not accord with the temper of Huaxu today. They are set down here only as a record of former times and ought not to be restored.

name: Field Notes on the Grand Incense Rite (Excerpt)
desc: A set of notes left by a foreign scholar investigating the origins of Huaxu's Grand Incense Rite. The date of composition is unknown. Many of the author's conjectures lack corroborating records or material evidence, and most of the text is not recognised as credible by modern historians.

res.text:
...

In sum, Huaxu's Grand Incense Rite is the country's most important recurring festival. Its ritual form has shifted over the centuries, yet the stages of that evolution are surprisingly well attested, each aligning with Huaxu's economic, technological, and artistic development at the time.

A plausible hypothesis is that the festival began as a large-scale rite unique to Huaxu. Over time, it adapted to the needs and conditions of each era, shedding many elements while preserving its essential core — through which the people of Huaxu give shape to a distinctive cultural identity.

The "divinities" worshipped by the people of Huaxu are not mere symbols. They exist, and they influence the ecology within Huaxu's borders in concrete, observable ways. I have personally witnessed the descent of the deity called Taihao during the Grand Incense Rite, and the experience left me profoundly shaken.

...

I am beginning to suspect a flaw in my earlier line of inquiry. I once assumed the Grand Incense Rite resembled festivals in other nations: cultural practices that grew out of commemoration and sacrifice, preserving certain customs as tradition. Ordinarily, such customs become simpler and more secularised as time advances.

Yet after examining every extant record of the Rite within Huaxu, I found that its central custom — the act of incense offering itself — has remained unchanged in both materials and quantity for nearly a thousand years of recorded history.

Given the manifest presence of "divine" power within Huaxu's territory, I have reason to believe the Rite is not merely a cultural or political form of worship. It may have a distinct functional purpose. Put plainly: in Huaxu, and only in Huaxu, a rite that exchanges offerings for a deity's protection appears to function as an actual transaction.

But why would Taihao require these incenses? And what, in fact, is Taihao? No comparable records exist elsewhere in Atlasia, and the incense used for such offerings is produced only within Huaxu... Incense found only here — and a "god" found only here that feeds upon it? The symmetry is too neat. It feels less like coincidence than design.

...

This functional reading suggests an intriguing possibility. Perhaps Huaxu's so-called "divinities" are not the exalted beings of popular imagination at all, but something closer to a machine — an apparatus that regulates the environment within its sphere of influence. It may even affect, or outright control, nearby Filthoids, pressing them into service as a blunt tool of enforcement. In that case, the Grand Incense Rite is less a ceremony than a scheduled procedure: refuelling this immense "machine" with what Huaxu calls "incense", at fixed intervals and in fixed amounts.

If this conjecture proves true, it would imply that, a thousand years ago, the people of Huaxu had mastered a technology capable of creating a "god". Should such a technology be deciphered, the Nine Chapters of Dafeng might be extended across Atlasia; or the mechanism's field of influence might be scaled down to the individual, enabling the creation of specialised protective devices.

Yet if such a technology truly exists, why does it function only within Huaxu's borders? Even the Starweavers have left no record of employing similar techniques beyond Huaxu’s border. What, then, is the crucial factor that imposes this limitation?

...

name: Qing's Wish
desc:
A tale of Yin Qing, a poet of ancient Huaxu, drawn from Bygone Fragments, an essay collection by the later author Cang Xian. In it, a young traveller known only as Feng — his family name now lost to history — drifts into Haojing and discovers a green leaf inscribed with a poem drifting along a waterway beside the Yin residence — a small happenstance that binds their fates.

preserves a number of literary anecdotes from roughly five centuries past, steeped in the flavour of legend. Its reliability as a historical source remains open to question, yet its value as literature is widely acknowledged.

res.text:
...

The leaf had long since turned yellow, yet the traces of ink upon it remained clear. Yin Qing studied it, gave a long, wistful sigh, and after a moment allowed himself a faint smile.
"I once wished to roam the world," he said to Feng, "yet my father and mother would not permit it. So I wrote upon this green leaf and set it adrift with the current, to ease my longing. Now that you have chanced upon it, carry it with you on your travels, that my wish may journey beside you."
Feng was silent for a long while. Then he replied,
"Why should we not travel together?"

...

When they reached the Lin River, Feng was stricken with a grave illness and lay bedridden. Qing said, "Rest now, and recover your strength. I shall remain here until you are well; then we shall set out again."
But Feng would not agree. He drew forth the withered leaf and pressed it into Qing's hand.
"Take this leaf," he said. "Go far. Let it be as though we still travel side by side."

...

Qing travelled far and wide, and in time he filled an entire chest with his verses. Wherever he went, he won admirers who pressed him to remain, yet he declined them all.
In his later years, he returned once more to the familiar banks of the Lin. Before Feng's grave, he buried the withered leaf in the soil and laid fresh green leaves above it.
Upon a leaf he inscribed two lines:

"Green leaves lie upon your grave;
The ache in my heart drifts with the stream."

name: Huaxu Trends – Haojing Special
desc:
Huaxu Trends tracks what's trending across Huaxu: new places to eat and drink, clothing and everyday essentials, and lifestyles arriving from overseas and taking hold at home.
Each year, the Haojing Special drops a month before the Grand Incense Rite, spotlighting the capital's latest go-to spots for food, leisure, and nightlife.

res.text:
Top Dining Pick: Bazhen Pavilion

In last month's reader poll, Bazhen Pavilion beat the runner-up by nearly a hundred votes — clearly a crowd favourite.

Our rule is simple: we don't recommend what we haven't tried. So we went in as ordinary diners and ordered the signature dishes. The fan-favourite Bazhen Tofu really is a standout: silky-soft, layered with flavour, and finished with a scatter of corn kernels — looks as good as it tastes.

Mistwharf Vinegar Fish is a classic, but the sharp vinegar tang isn't for everyone, especially with freshwater fish. A couple of us left it unfinished.

...

From Diner A: Chef Bai's cooking speaks for itself. And Chef Li isn't far behind. Word is his poems are just as good as his food.

From Diner B: When I was young, my family always celebrated my birthday at Bazhen Pavilion... Years have gone by. Though the people who once sat beside me are no longer with me, the dishes taste the same. And perhaps that is enough.

From Diner C: Whenever friends or relatives visit Haojing, Bazhen Pavilion is the first place I take them. That said, lately some of the new dishes feel like they're trying a little too hard to please out-of-towners. It's not quite the same as it used to be — not that there's anything wrong with catering to visitors.

...

name: Ode to the Nine Chapters
desc:
A short piece praising the Nine Chapters of Dafeng, written in Huaxu's distinctive panegyric style.
From the wording and the marginal note appended below, the author appears to be a student still learning the craft of writing.

name: A Compendium of Incense
desc: A celebrated Huaxu classic, reputedly written by a master of Xuanheng Sect. The work runs to seventeen volumes, with additions made by later generations. The excerpt below is drawn from the book's preface.

res.text:
The art of incense has changed with the ages. In antiquity, aromatic herbs were burnt to raise fragrant smoke to reach the divine; in the present age, incense is measured and its vapours harmonised, so that by this craft the Mandate of Heaven may be set in order.

The Record of Yang's Life relates that at the founding of the Nine Chapters, Yang declared: "When the Mandate of Heaven intermingles, all courses are impeded, and what is tangled cannot easily be loosed." She therefore sent men to gather a myriad of aromatics and heap them at the Taixu Mausoleum, where they were burnt without cease, day and night. Yang herself sat beside the pyre. When the smoke ran thick, none could draw near; and when at last it thinned, she had vanished.

This account need not be taken on faith. Versions differ from place to place, and much has shifted with the passing of years. I compile this book not to quarrel over such tales, but to set down the incense arts of Huaxu across the span of ages. Within these pages I have gathered, as exhaustively as I could, matters of Heaven and Earth, of human affairs and the produce of the land; what was ancient is collected, and what is current is brought within its compass. It is my hope that those who come after may follow this lineage, and enrich it in their turn.

The whole consists of seventeen volumes. The first nine record the incense materials: orchid and fragrant herb, pepper and cassia, aloeswood, sandalwood, borneol and musk — ancient varieties of Huaxu — together with rare foreign aromatics once presented as tribute.

Marginal note: Since the widening of the Starweavers' routes, what was once unheard-of has become obtainable.

The next four volumes treat of the uses of incense. Incense serves many ends: for offering, for wear, and for medicine. These are set out in detail below.

The final three volumes concern the art of incense blending. Though its principles may appear simple, it is in truth the most demanding of all related crafts. One must first master the preceding thirteen volumes and commit them thoroughly to memory; only then may one properly undertake this discipline.

The uses of incense are as boundless as the sea, and their subtleties are still beyond our full grasp. I have done no more than gather and preserve a handful of remarkable formulae devised by sages of old, that their methods might endure.

name: A Match Made
desc: A folk opera script popular among Huaxu's commoners. It follows a young couple from first meeting to marriage, only for petty quarrels and everyday slights to sour things afterwards. Said to be adapted from a real case in Haojing, though this cannot be verified. Excerpt follows.

res.text:
No need for the Moon Matchmaker to meddle. One red thread binds the romance. The crimson bridal sedan chair halts at the gate. Whether she wills it or no — gown on, veil down — once she mounts, the union is sealed. A hundred hands bear it onwards. The bridegroom reels, heart unmoored, as though he had glimpsed a heavenly maiden in a dream.

(Offstage, a hurried reply.)
Jing (beaming): Splendid! Good luck upon good luck — three cups for that!
Mo: It's late. My lady is waiting. I'll be taking my leave.
Jing: Nonsense! You've drained more cups than I can count at the Bazhen Pavilion and never once been drunk. And now you're baulking at a single cup? You'll be the laughingstock!
Mo: Things aren't what they were. Don't take it amiss, brother.
(Mo bows with clasped hands.)
Jing (laughing): Ha! And here I thought you were a man of mettle — turns out you go to ground the moment wine's poured.
Jing: Fine, fine. If he's that set on ducking out, no need to push it.
Mo (startled): Why would you say that? All these years of brotherhood, and you'd throw it away over one cup of wine?
Jing: Brotherhood? If that means anything to you — today's your wedding day, everyone's here to toast you. And you won't drink a single cup with us?
All: Hear, hear!
Jing: Some loyalty. Some brother.
All: Hear, hear!
Mo (sighing): Pomegranate blazes red as fire... and still, it cannot match the bitter smoke of mugwort... Ah, well.
Mo (raising his voice): Today I'll drink with you if it kills me. Gentlemen — your health!
(All drink.)

A crescent moon crests the little tower, yet its tender light falls only into the gutter. Hair dressed in vain, pipa in hand... whose ear awaits her song?

name: Hall of Craft Annual Record: Works Digest
desc: A substantial volume detailing the Ministry of Works' most recent public projects.

res.text:
The Ministry of Works hereby announces the following works under its charge:

Ⅰ. Rehabilitation of Official Roads
By order, the city's principal roads and minor roads are to be repaired and reinforced. Roadbeds shall be strengthened and carriageways widened, easing the passage of carts and riders and improving travel throughout the city, so that the routes may run clear in all directions.

Ⅱ. Construction of Freight-Handling Apparatus
New freight-handling apparatus shall be constructed, with a wrought-iron frame and precision gearing. Efficiency shall be improved and operations standardised, speeding the circulation of goods and encouraging commercial growth.

Ⅲ. Reinforcement and Repair of the Wharves
The existing wharves shall undergo full inspection and repair. Riverbanks shall be reinforced, rotted timbers replaced, and additional safeguards installed, ensuring safe passage for vessels and keeping grain transport secure.

...

All works shall be carried out in accordance with established codes: rooted in traditional practice, yet open to new techniques. The Ministry of Works faithfully discharges its duty, securing the foundations of the state and serving the needs of the people.

Those wishing to consult the full project files may do so in the Ministry's archives.

name: The Sayings of Master Zhuxi
desc: A record of Master Zhuxi's sayings, written down by his students. His views shifted with age, yet his words were preserved throughout his life, from his earliest years to his last. Excerpt follows.

res.text:
In considering what the sages of old intended when they taught learning, I take it to be this: to press inquiry to its limits, and to read widely in the old and the new, so as to broaden the mind and enlarge one's view. Only then may a person judge right from wrong, weigh matters with clarity, and grasp the workings of the world — not merely memorise texts and polish fine phrases for the sake of fame, profit, and preferment.

Those who study in our day have borne hardships for too long. Much of what the former worthies taught is recorded in the classics, yet remains detached from worldly affairs. Anyone with resolve ought to read deeply, reflect, and question — to examine and sift what one has learned. For if one recognises the vastness of Heaven and Earth and the complexity of affairs, and strives to look upon all things with objectivity and a mind trained to weigh matters with discernment, then the standards by which one stands in the world and conducts oneself are already within one's grasp. Why wait for others to hand them over before one can hold fast to them?

As for what I have written, it cannot guide every student, and the methods it proposes may not fully accord with the true aim of opening the mind and awakening thought. Therefore I shall no longer require it in this hall. Instead, I have selected the main principles by which the sages taught learning, set them forth as articles, and posted them here for all to see. Let all of you study them together, make their meaning clear, keep them, and hold yourselves to them. Then, in the midst of your thoughts and actions, your judgement will grow more exacting: you will deliberate with care, discern with clarity, and investigate things so as to extend your knowledge. These are, in truth, the roots of conduct in the world, and the foundations of cultivating virtue and turning towards the good.

Only by keeping to this guiding framework may one contemplate all things, and so bring forth new understanding and open new paths.

name: Workshop Experiment Log
desc: A workshop logbook where Outer Peaks' artisans jot down their wild ideas and odd contraptions. In the name of "learning from one another", Uncle Tang later insisted on adding a comment board so everyone could leave their thoughts underneath.

res.text:
I. Meowvellous Machine

Logged by: Uncle Tang (love you lot, everyone in Outer Peaks!)

Setup:
Split the kids into two groups. One got a pep talk from the Meowvellous Machine beforehand; the other didn't.
Both groups then read Mechanism Basics That Every Huaxu Kid Can Learn. After one stick of incense, we gave them a quiz.

Result:
Some of the "encouraged" kids (Zhu Pu, for instance) made the top ten. Others landed near the bottom. The kids who didn't get the pep talk (like Pei Jing) ended up somewhere in the middle.

Comments:
Su Yi: The groups weren't evenly matched to begin with. The results don't prove anything.
Xu Hong: I think some of them were just scared by how the machine looks.
Kezhou: The results aren't the point. I just want to ask... what's with that signature in the "Logged by" line? Has Uncle Tang been breathing in workshop fumes again?


II. Duck and Dash

Logged by: Uncle Tang (still loving you lot today)

Setup:
After basic safety checks, we went out into the wild. On spotting a lone Sable Bi'an, give a Duck and Dash a full wind and toss it.

Result:
Didn't scare it off. If anything, it made so much noise that it drew more of them in and made them meaner.

Areas to Improve:
Try making it even louder.

Comments:
Su Yi: Why not pack it with a few small charges? Like the firecrackers we set off at New Year — toss it, then leg it while it's popping.
Uncle Tang: This is meant for schoolchildren to use for self-defence on the way home. If we add anything like that, I'm worried they'll misuse it and hurt themselves.
Shen Han: Are the children all right? No one was hurt, I hope? Uncle Tang — please don't drag them into such dangerous experiments next time!

name: The Incense Trial: The Civil Service Exam in Smoke and Scent
desc: An anonymous miscellany from Huaxu, offering a detailed account of the rules and procedures of the Incense Trial.

res.text:
Within Huaxu's system of governance, few institutions are as distinctive as the Incense Trial — an annual examination established by the Ministry of Rites to seek out promising talent among the young. Built around Huaxu's own incense culture, it proceeds in stages, each stricter than the last. Learning is tested openly; character and suitability are weighed more quietly. In time, it has become a signature feature of Huaxu's governance.

Shrine Trial — Timed by Smoke, Judged by Learning
The selection begins with the Shrine Trial, a small regional examination held throughout Huaxu. Each sitting is held at the district's Argent Loong Temple: a first-round screening, and a gesture of reverence to Lord Argent. The trial is conducted inside the temple itself, overseen by the temple's incense wardens, who are charged with keeping order and impartiality from start to finish.
There is no interview at this stage; the focus is purely on a candidate's learning. On the appointed day, candidates enter with their admission slips and take their seats. Writing materials are issued, but no one may touch brush to paper until permitted. Only when the supervising warden lights the designated Lunarose incense, and the candidates have completed their rite of thanks to Lord Argent, does the examination begin in earnest. The time allowed is exactly the burn of a single stick of Lunarose incense.
The top three from each sitting advance, and must in due course travel to Huaxu's capital, Haojing, for a harsher round of selection.

Departmental Trial — Matched to Post, Weighed in Talent and Virtue
Candidates who reach Haojing then face the Departmental Trial, where suitability is the core concern. Unlike the Shrine Trial, which leans on written testing, this stage is not centred on the brush alone. Greater weight is placed on practical ability and how well a candidate fits the duties of the post. Interviews allow examiners to judge a candidate's speech, thinking, and character at closer range. Before sitting the trial, candidates must state their intended post, making an initial choice among the Three Ministries and their subordinate departments. The assessment shifts accordingly, depending on the functions of the chosen institution.
The close of the Departmental Trial marks the end of that year's Incense Trial. Once the list of successful candidates is confirmed, the Ministry of Rites summons all qualified entrants to the Hall of Adjudication to take up their appointments. Those whose talent and conduct are deemed exceptional may even win the favour of Lord Argent. In such cases, a Bi'an delivers a summons, granting leave to advance to a third stage: a final selection for the office of High Chancellor of Loongyuan.
During this interval, the Hall of Adjudication enters a brief recess to prepare postings and the High Chancellor selection to follow. Meanwhile, the Hall of Incense hastens its own preparations, assembling special aromatics reserved solely for the High Chancellor's selection.

As for how the High Chancellor of Loongyuan is ultimately chosen — Huaxu has no shortage of opinions. I have only learned that an internal procedure does exist, and that it is said to be fairly comprehensive.
For reasons of space, however, we'll leave Loongyuan for the next issue.

name: How to Become High Chancellor of Loongyuan
desc: A tongue-in-cheek essay that claims to explain how to become High Chancellor of Loongyuan. So exaggerated and irreverent that it's hard to tell where fact ends and invention begins.

res.text:
Do you want to become High Chancellor of Loongyuan?
Let me be specific: set aside the tangled official duties the post entails. Imagine instead that you keep the title and bask in universal admiration across Huaxu without having to lift a finger. Under those conditions, do you want it?
I expect most answers would be: of course!
Which brings us to the real question: how does one actually become High Chancellor of Loongyuan?

In last issue, we touched on the Incense Trial — the examination system by which the state selects officials from among the common run of Huaxu's citizens. But what of those so-called prodigies, the dazzling geniuses beyond the common measure? Is there a special track reserved for them? Are they appointed the moment they first wail into the world?
Certainly not.
Becoming High Chancellor of Loongyuan is no simple matter. Most readers will have guessed correctly: those singled out do indeed receive a message from Lord Argent — delivered, of course, by a Bi'an. But don't celebrate just yet. Receiving the message does not mean you've already made it. All it gives you is a new label: Candidate for High Chancellor of Loongyuan.
You answer the summons and travel to Haojing. There, the sitting High Chancellor receives you with great warmth. You gather in the Hall of Adjudication and talk — perhaps of state affairs, perhaps simply of daily life. This stage has a name: "The Trial of the Way."
When it ends, you are escorted back to your temporary quarters at the posting station to await the next summons.
And you wait.
Days pass. You pace like a cat on a hot tin roof, opening the door every few moments to see whether someone has come with news. The good news is that someone eventually does. If they didn't, this essay would end here — and then what would you do with your evening?

Filled with anticipation, you return once more to the Hall of Adjudication. You assume that since your previous examiner was the sitting High Chancellor of Loongyuan, this time you must surely meet Lord Argent themselves. But upon arrival, you notice there is no Lord Argent, nor the High Chancellor. Instead, a handful of Hall staffers hurriedly thrust an enormous stack of dossiers into your arms and then flee at once, as if the building is about to collapse.
Now comes your task: in this sea of records, you must trace the links between designated incidents and present your own reasoned conclusions. Someone will see to your meals, your lodging, your daily needs. You, however, are strictly forbidden from cutting corners. Try to slack off and you will be struck from the candidate list without ceremony.
This stage is called "The Trial of Statecraft."
Naturally, you are exceptional. After what feels like years poring over records — memorising every last petty detail from the past twenty years — you finally receive word one morning: you passed. The Trial of Statecraft is complete. Next comes, supposedly, an audience with Lord Argent.
You are beside yourself. You rush to Qianxiu Pavilion to have a new set of robes made — something bright and showy for the occasion. How many people go their entire lives without hearing even a single true word from Lord Argent? And you — you might see Them with your own eyes. What fortune beyond measure!
Unable to contain your excitement, you tell the shop assistant exactly why you are having clothes made. The girl takes one look at your glowing face and cannot help it: she covers her mouth and giggles.
"You know," she says, "not every candidate gets to see Lord Argent."
You go pale. You are just about to seek a further explanation when a messenger arrives with urgent orders: report to the Hall of Adjudication at once and prepare for the Trial of the Heart. With no time to dig, you hurriedly straighten your robes and make your way back to that now-familiar place.

Inside, incense smoke curls through the Hall — thick enough to be seen, yet without the faintest scent. This seems odd. An attendant arrives and has you sit on a cushion with the other candidates, instructing you to meditate and regulate your breath. Suspicious but obedient, you sit. Smoke coils around your eyes and nose. Your thoughts grow heavy. Drowsiness steals over you. You think you might as well close your eyes for a moment. So you do.
And you fall asleep.
You dream a long dream.
In it, you see your past: your mother cradling you, your father lifting you high above his head.
In it, you see your future: you succeed to the post of High Chancellor of Loongyuan, spend a lifetime wringing yourself dry for the people of Huaxu, and at last are laid to rest in the Taixu Mausoleum.
In it, you see others — countless faces, countless eyes fixed upon you. Questions rise, one after another, pressing and demanding. You are flustered, drenched in sweat, pushed to the brink — and then you jolt awake.
You look up. The incense lit at the beginning has not yet burned out.

In the end, you do not pass the selection. Presumably, your performance in the dream failed to please Lord Argent. Still, though not chosen, you ultimately join the Hall of Incense and continue serving the people of Huaxu. A happy ending all the same, wouldn't you say?

And so, dear readers, you now know exactly how to become High Chancellor of Loongyuan. And if one of you actually does make it to High Chancellor someday... well, I trust you'll remember me, the humble author who wrote this helpful little piece. A little token of appreciation sent my way would not go amiss. Don't you think?

name: Dawn of Haojing
desc: A daily paper printed by the Hall of Craft and sold on the streets of Haojing. Mostly local happenings and the occasional public notice. Truth be told, it has never had many readers.

res.name: Dawn of Haojing — Issue Ⅰ
res.text:
Ⅰ. East Market: Floodwater Half-Drowns a Lord Argent Statue

After days of relentless rain, Haojing Lake rose fast enough to spill over the East Market embankment. One shopkeeper, known locally for his devotion, kept a three-foot wooden statue of Lord Argent at his shopfront and burnt incense to it each day without fail.
Early one morning, a shophand named Zhang opened up the shop to sweep the threshold — only to find the water already lapping at the steps, the statue's lower half swallowed up. Startled, Zhang shouted for help, and the neighbours together hauled the image further inside.
Tongues wag: "Lord Argent's ways are inscrutable." Surely this is Their doing — making plain Their displeasure at private offerings by flooding Their own image, a stark reminder to respect the seasons and Heaven's will.


Ⅱ. Astonishing: Sixty-Two-Year-Old Widow Gives Birth

Mrs Liu of Haojing, a widow of sixty-two, has long lived alone and childless, and in her quiet days was often lonely.
In recent months, she complained frequently of fatigue and found her appetite greatly increased. Neighbours took it for the usual signs of age. No one expected what came after: on the nineteenth of this month, she gave birth to a baby boy — loud-voiced when he cried, bright-eyed, and fine-featured.
Word soon reached the Hall of Founts, which sent an officer to verify the matter. Mrs Liu claims that three months ago she dreamt of a woman in blue who offered her a peach, sweet beyond telling; upon waking, she felt her body begin to change. The child bears a faint red birthmark at the waist, shaped unmistakably like a peach — proof that the dream was no mere fancy.
Strange indeed. Such tales belong, people say, to storybooks — not to everyday life. The neighbours insist Mrs Liu has always been known for kindness, and some whisper that Heaven, in its own way, repays the virtuous.
The Hall of Founts has registered the child and granted assistance in grain and bolts of cloth. Friends and relations arrive daily with congratulations, and curious onlookers have been gathering in no small numbers.


Ⅲ. West Market Oddity: A Dog That Hunts Rats

At the West Market eatery Baiwei House, the proprietor Li Sanlang keeps a yellow dog named Rusty to mind the place at night. He has been a good dog: quiet, steady, and has never caused trouble.
On the afternoon of the first of this month, the shophands were airing out dried ingredients in the sun when Rusty suddenly wouldn't stop barking. They hurried over and saw him dart to a rat hole at the base of the wall. A moment later he came back out with a grey rat clenched in his jaws, already dead.
Taken aback, the hands reported it to Li Sanlang. Li wouldn't believe a word of it — until the next day, when he saw it with his own eyes: Rusty crouched by the hole, and the moment a rat poked its head out, he lunged. Before the day was out, he'd caught three. One regular laughed: "The old saying compares a dog that catches mice to nosy folk who meddle in other people's business — but it's a blessing when your place is full of rats."
Since then, Rusty has hunted rats by day and kept watch by night. Baiwei House, it is said, has had no trouble with rats since.

Ⅱ. Unrest on the Western Outskirts — Drifters Sighted Again?

In recent days, citizens have been arriving at the Ministry of Fortune in growing numbers, reporting that along the back paths of the western outskirts, shadowy figures have been seen lingering. Those who claim to have spoken with them describe shifty replies and evasive eyes — hardly the bearing of decent folk. It is feared some mischief is being plotted in secret.
Though Huaxu stands under the protection of the Nine Chapters of Dafeng, Drifters have long been said to lurk even within Haojing, committing offence upon offence. A censer that had burned unbroken for a hundred years was once extinguished — doused with water by the most notorious of their lot. Another drove a mechapuppet straight into the Hall of Adjudication. Others have hung wenzhu fronds outside people's doors to mark their targets, then ambushed them and left them bleeding. Their crimes are many; their wickedness unrepentant.
Even so, there are always those who make excuses for them, shielding them in the dark and dressing them up with fine names like the Four Drifters. Fortunately, the Magistrates of Yingtian took action, and the so-called Four Drifters were seized and put to death.
Yet though their ringleaders and close followers have been dealt with, remnants are said to remain. The people fear renewed Drifter activity may flare again and bring fresh calamity.
The Hall of Adjudication has therefore issued the following order: the Magistrates' patrols are to be strengthened at once. A reward of 12,000 is hereby offered for any report of Drifters' whereabouts that is verified. Residents are further warned: do not enter desolate places after nightfall. Every measure is to be taken to root out the Drifters.

name: Notes on the Mirage (Ⅱ)
desc: A book set down by a man of letters surnamed Shen. Its authenticity cannot be verified, but it remains an entertaining read. Much of the text has been lost to time. This is Part Ⅱ.

res.text:
On the surface of Haojing Lake, mist sometimes gathers into shapes — towers, palaces, immortals, spectres — each outlined with startling clarity. People call such sights the Mirage. Some say it is Lord Argent's breath; others insist it is the work of Lord Argent's eight immortal attendants. Accounts multiply without end. I doubt them all.

I chased down every rumour I could find, yet reached no firm conclusion. I went about the city seeking out the elders, asking how one might reach the Mirage, and I began with the boatmen, hoping they would row me across the lake in search of it. They mocked my folly — yet they agreed readily once paid, and accompanied me on several trips. Back and forth we went, again and again, and still we found nothing.

I searched daily until my meagre means were spent. A few, taking pity, would join me in their spare hours, though their earlier enthusiasm was gone. I did not resent them; I felt only shame. In the end I put what little remained to my name into buying a bamboo raft, resolved to seek the Mirage on my own.

Though I am but a bookish sort, I grew up climbing hills and swimming rivers with the neighbourhood boys. I am no weakling — yet my skills go no further than that. At first, poling the raft was awkward and stiff; with time I grew steadily more practised.

The search proved arduous indeed. At first I tried to take my bearings and fix a heading. Later there was only the endless expanse, drifting and bobbing with the waves. Still I never beheld the Mirage's true face. In time my spirit faltered. I began to suspect I was clinging to emptiness, wasting my days and wearing down my resolve. Now and then I would glimpse it in the distance and strain towards it, only for it to vanish the moment I drew near — like moonlight on water, dissolving into nothing at the slightest touch.

One day a thick fog rolled in over Haojing, and I could not make out a person two steps away. Everyone warned me not to go, fearing I would lose my way on the lake and die there. I sighed and said, "Other than my life, what do I have left to lose?" My purse was already empty. We scraped by on my wife's needlework. Thankfully we had no children; otherwise, what kind of husband would that make me?

Still I insisted on leaving. My wife wept and tried to stop me. "If you step out that door," she said, "I will never be your wife again." My resolve faltered — yet in the end I steeled myself, flung the door wide, and went.

The fog blotted out heaven and earth. When the tip of my pole struck the water, I could not even see where it fell. I could only feel the raft's motion through my wrists. The cold was sharper than on any ordinary day; it cut to the bone. Frost gathered in my beard; I breathed it away, and moments later it formed again.

Nothing about the scene seemed especially strange. Perhaps there was something wondrous, yet my mind was so muddled that I could not recall it. I remember only one instant: at one point it felt as though my pole was no longer meeting water at all, but something lighter — like pushing through cloud. A feeling too surreal for words to depict.

I cannot say how long I went on. Then the fog began to thin. Before me, overlapping haloes of light shimmered, and within them rose halls and pavilions, radiant beyond measure. Joy seized me like a fever. I gathered what strength remained and drove the raft forward. Just as my strength drained, the raft struck shore. It was as though a stone had finally dropped from my chest. My heart, at last, began to steady.

I left the raft behind and stepped ashore. The ground beneath my feet felt soft as water, yet I neither sank nor grew wet. With each step, ripples spread outward. It was wonder that defied belief.

name: 遗落的纸张·皓京
desc: A collection of enigmatic pages discovered by chance. Some are delicate scrolls of fine parchment; others, freshly printed sheets with ink still crisp and dark. A few are no more than torn scraps from half-used notebooks. Whether neatly penned or barely legible, they all share one thing in common — each contains a hint pointing to the whereabouts of a hidden treasure.

res.name: 皓京·其一
res.text:
椒桂沉檀馨香好，兰蕙脑麝馥郁浓。
借问宝物何处寻，牧童遥指金庭树。

res.name: 皓京·其二
res.text:
东指郊外草渐深，没入窟中寻不得。
盼星望月痴等寻，却探宝物根深藏。

res.name: 皓京·其三
res.text:
南来又北往，东过又西寻。
联西处，通中城，问宝物何在？涸木之下水之上。
